In [[Canada]], [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Indigenous peoples]] (also known as Aboriginal Canadians)<ref name="indian" /> represent roughly 5% of the [[Population of Canada|overall population]]. They comprise the [[Inuit]],<ref name="ICCcharter">{{cite web|title = Inuit Circumpolar Council (Canada)-ICC Charter| work = Inuit Circumpolar Council > ICC Charter and By-laws > ICC Charter| year = 2007| url = http://inuitcircumpolar.com/index.php?auto_slide=&ID=374&Lang=En&Parent_ID=&current_slide_num=| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070928132218/http://inuitcircumpolar.com/index.php?auto_slide=&ID=374&Lang=En&Parent_ID=&current_slide_num= | archive-date = September 28, 2007| access-date =September 18, 2009 }}</ref> [[Métis#Métis people in Canada|Métis]],{{sfn|Todd|Thornton|Collins|2001|p=10}} and [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]],<ref name="First Nations Culture Areas Index">{{cite web| title = Civilization.ca-Gateway to Aboriginal Heritage-Culture| work = Canadian Museum of Civilization Corporation| publisher = Government of Canada| date = May 12, 2006| url = http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/tresors/ethno/etb0170e.shtml| access-date =September 18, 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091020033621/http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/tresors/ethno/etb0170e.shtml| archive-date= October 20, 2009 <!--scSHBot-->| url-status=live}}</ref> of which there are over 600 recognized [[List of First Nations peoples in Canada|First Nations governments]] or [[Band government|bands]] with distinctive cultures, languages, music and arts.<ref name="Aboriginal Identity 2011">[http://www.statcan.gc.ca/daily-quotidien/130508/dq130508a-eng.htm?HPA 2011 National Household Survey: Indigenous Peoples in Canada: First Nations People, Métis and Inuit]</ref><ref name="three2">{{cite web| title = Civilization.ca-Gateway to Aboriginal Heritage-object| publisher = Canadian Museum of Civilization Corporation| date = May 12, 2006| url = http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/tresors/ethno/etb0000e.shtml| access-date =October 2, 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091015074407/http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/tresors/ethno/etb0000e.shtml| archive-date=October 15, 2009| url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Old Crow Flats]] and [[Bluefish Caves]] are some of the earliest known sites of human habitation in Canada.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bluefish Caves |url=https://kgs.ku.edu/bluefish-caves#:~:text=The%20Bluefish%20Caves%20site%20in,the%20Archaeological%20Survey%20of%20Canada. |access-date=2025-05-13 |website=kgs.ku.edu |language=en}}</ref> The characteristics of Indigenous cultures in Canada prior to European colonization included permanent settlements,<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lwqYG0VJC7UC&q=Invisible%20genealogies%3A%20a%20history%20of%20Americanist%20anthropology%20%20By%20Regna%20Darnell&pg=PA338|title=Invisible genealogies: a history of Americanist anthropology|first=Regna|last=Darnell|year=2001|location=Lincoln, Nebraska|publisher=University of Nebraska Press|isbn=978-0-8032-1710-2|access-date=October 3, 2010}}</ref> possibly agriculture,<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aEHX63g1XsYC&q=A%20concise%20economic%20history%20of%20the%20world%3A%20from%20Paleolithic%20times%20to%20the%20present%20%20By%20Rondo%20E.%20Cameron&pg=PA92|title=A concise economic history of the world: from Paleolithic times to the present|first=Rondo E.|last=Cameron|year=1993|publisher=Oxford University Press|page=92|isbn=978-0-19-507445-1|access-date=October 3, 2010}}</ref> civic and ceremonial architecture,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kalman|first1=Harold|last2=Mills|first2=Edward|title=Architectural History: Early First Nations|url=http://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.com/en/article/architectural-history-early-first-nations/|publisher=The Canadian Encyclopedia (Historica-Dominion)|date=September 30, 2007|access-date=November 27, 2013}}</ref> complex [[Hierarchy|societal hierarchies]], and [[Trade|trading networks]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=quM1xyFyfhQC&q=indigenous%20difference%20and%20the%20Constitution%20of%20Canada%20By%20Patrick%20Macklem&pg=PA170|title=Indigenous difference and the Constitution of Canada|first=Patrick|last=Macklem|year=2001|publisher=University of Toronto Press|page=170|isbn=978-0-8020-4195-1|access-date=October 3, 2010}}</ref> Métis nations of mixed ancestry originated in the mid-17th century when First Nations and Inuit married Europeans, primarily [[French colonization of the Americas|French settlers]].<ref name=testt/> First Nations and Métis peoples played a critical part in the development of European colonies in Canada, particularly for their role in assisting Europeans during the [[North American fur trade]].

Various [[Canadian Aboriginal law|Aboriginal laws]], [[Treaty#Canada|treaties]], and legislation have been enacted between European immigrants and Indigenous groups across Canada. The impact of [[settler colonialism in Canada]] can be seen in its culture, history, politics, laws, and legislatures.<ref name="y517">{{cite book |last=Reynolds |first=J. |title=Canada and Colonialism: An Unfinished History |publisher=[[University of British Columbia Press]] |year=2024 |isbn=978-0-7748-8096-1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b7wIEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA3 |pages=3–10}}</ref> Historically, this included assimilationist policies affecting Indigenous languages, traditions, religion and the degradation of Indigenous communities that has contemporarily been described by some, including academics and politicians, as a [[Canadian genocide of Indigenous peoples|cultural genocide or genocide]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Woolford |first1=Andrew |title=Ontological Destruction: Genocide and Canadian Aboriginal Peoples |journal=[[Genocide Studies and Prevention]] |date=2009 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=81–97 |doi=10.3138/gsp.4.1.81}};  {{cite journal |last=Green |first=Robyn |date=December 2015 |title=The economics of reconciliation: tracing investment in Indigenous–settler relations |journal=[[Journal of Genocide Research]] |volume=17 |number=4 |pages=473–493 |doi=10.1080/14623528.2015.1096582}};  {{cite journal |last1=MacDonald |first1=David B. |author1-link=David Bruce MacDonald |last2=Hudson |first2=Graham |date=2012 |title=The Genocide Question and Indian Residential Schools in Canada |journal=[[Canadian Journal of Political Science]] |volume=45|number=2|doi=10.1017/s000842391200039x|pages=430–431}}; {{cite journal |last=Dhamoon |first=Rita Kaur |date=2016 |title=Re-presenting Genocide: The Canadian Museum of Human Rights and Settler Colonial Power |journal=The Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics |volume=1 |number=1 |doi=10.1017/rep.2015.4|page=10}}; {{cite encyclopedia |title=Genocide and Indigenous Peoples in Canada |encyclopedia=[[The Canadian Encyclopedia]] |date=November 2, 2020 |url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/genocide-and-indigenous-peoples-in-canada |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240802020743/https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/genocide-and-indigenous-peoples-in-canada |archive-date=August 2, 2024}}</ref>

The modern Indigenous right to [[Self-governance|self-government]] provides for [[Indigenous self-government in Canada]] and the management of cultural, political, health and economic responsibilities within Indigenous communities. [[National Indigenous Peoples Day]] recognizes the vast cultures and contributions of Indigenous peoples to the [[history of Canada]].<ref name=history/> First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples of all backgrounds have become [[Indigenous Canadian personalities|prominent figures]] in Canada and have helped shape the [[Culture of Canada|Canadian cultural identity]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.naaf.ca/program/92|work=National Aboriginal Achievement Foundation|title=National Aboriginal Achievement Award Recipients | access-date =October 7, 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091011015233/http://www.naaf.ca/program/92| archive-date=October 11, 2009| url-status=live}}</ref>

==Terminology==
[[File:Native_Americans_Race.svg|thumb|Indigenous peoples in [[Canada]] and the [[United States]], % of population by area.]]

In [[Section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982|Section 35]] of the ''[[Constitution Act, 1982]]'', "Aboriginal peoples of Canada" includes [[First Nations in Canada|Indian]], [[Inuit]], and [[Métis]] peoples.<ref name="defe">{{cite web| title = Constitution Act, 1982 Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms| work = Department of Justice| publisher = Government of Canada| year = 1982| url = http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/ca_1982.html| access-date =October 5, 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091021182217/http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/ca_1982.html| archive-date=October 21, 2009| url-status=live}}</ref>  "Aboriginal" as a [[collective noun]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/indigenous-aboriginal-which-is-correct-1.3771433 |title= Indigenous or Aboriginal: Which is correct? | date =September 21, 2016|access-date=November 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160922085332/https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/indigenous-aboriginal-which-is-correct-1.3771433 |archive-date=September 22, 2016}}</ref> is a specific [[Jargon|term of art]] used as a legal term encompassing all Indigenous peoples living in Canada.<ref name=term>{{cite web|url=http://www.aidp.bc.ca/terminology_of_native_aboriginal_metis.pdf |title=Terminology of First Nations, Native, Aboriginal and Metis (NAHO) |work=aidp.bc.ca/ |access-date=October 5, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100714021655/http://www.aidp.bc.ca/terminology_of_native_aboriginal_metis.pdf |archive-date=July 14, 2010  }}</ref><ref name=Terminology>{{cite web|url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ap/tln-eng.asp|title=Terminology|work=Indian and Northern Affairs Canada| access-date =October 5, 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091027041022/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ap/tln-eng.asp| archive-date=October 27, 2009| url-status=live}}</ref> Although "Indian" is a term still commonly used in legal documents for First Nations, the descriptors "Indian" and "[[Eskimo]]" have fallen into disuse in Canada; most consider them to be [[pejorative]].<ref name="indian" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Words First An Evolving Terminology Relating to Indigenous peoples in Canada |url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/pr/pub/wf/trmrslt_e.asp?term=12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030106123913/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/pr/pub/wf/trmrslt_e.asp?term=12 |archive-date=January 6, 2003 |publisher=Communications Branch of Indian and Northern Affairs Canada |year=2004 |access-date=June 26, 2010}}</ref>{{sfn|Olson|Pappas|1994|p=213}} ''Indian'' remains in place as the legal term used in the [[Constitution of Canada|Canadian Constitution]].<ref name="indian"/>{{efn|''Indian'' is used here because of the historical nature of the article and the precision of the name, as with [[Indian hospital]].<ref name=Indian>{{cite web|title=Terminology Guide: Research on Aboriginal Heritage|url=https://www.bac-lac.gc.ca/eng/discover/aboriginal-heritage/Documents/Terminology%20Guide%20%20Aboriginal%20Heritage.pdf|publisher = Library and Archives Canada |date=2012|accessdate=April 8, 2023}}</ref> It was, and continues to be, used by government officials, Indigenous peoples and historians while referencing the school system. The use of the name also provides relevant context about the era in which the system was established, specifically one in which Indigenous peoples in Canada were homogeneously referred to as ''Indians'' rather than by language that distinguishes [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]], [[Inuit]] and [[Métis]] peoples.<ref name=Indian/> Use of ''Indian'' is limited throughout the article to proper nouns and references to government legislation.}} ''Aboriginal peoples'' has begun to be considered outdated and is slowly being replaced by the term ''Indigenous peoples''.{{efn|The words ''Aboriginal'' and ''Indigenous'' are capitalized when used in a Canadian context.<ref name="v778">{{cite web | title=The Canadian Style | website=TERMIUM Plus® | date=October 8, 2009 | url=https://www.btb.termiumplus.gc.ca/tcdnstyl-chap?lang=eng&lettr=chap_catlog&info0=14 | access-date=July 16, 2024}}</ref><ref name="j729">{{cite web | title=4.11 Races, languages and peoples, 4.12 | website=TERMIUM Plus® | date=October 8, 2009 | url=https://www.btb.termiumplus.gc.ca/tcdnstyl-chap?lang=eng&lettr=indx_catlog&info0=4.11&info1=4.12 | access-date=July 16, 2024}}</ref><ref name="s316">{{cite web | title=Indigenous Peoples | website=University of Guelph | date=November 14, 2019 | url=https://news.uoguelph.ca/guides/style-guide/inclusive-language/indigenous-peoples/ | access-date=July 24, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=14.12 Elimination of Racial and Ethnic Stereotyping, Identification of Groups|url=https://www.btb.termiumplus.gc.ca/tcdnstyl-srch?lang=eng&srchtxt=indigenous&cur=2&nmbr=2&lettr=14&info0=14.12#zz14|website=Translation Bureau|publisher=Public Works and Government Services Canada|access-date=July 2, 2020|language=en|year=2017}}</ref><ref name="McKay">{{cite web|last1=McKay |first1=Celeste |title=Briefing Note on Terminology |url=http://umanitoba.ca/student/indigenous/terminology.html |publisher=University of Manitoba |access-date=July 2, 2020 |date=April 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161025224808/http://umanitoba.ca/student/indigenous/terminology.html |archive-date=October 25, 2016 }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Todorova|first=Miglena|date=2016|title=Co-Created Learning: Decolonizing Journalism Education in Canada|journal=Canadian Journal of Communication|volume=41|issue=4|pages=673–92|doi=10.22230/cjc.2016v41n4a2970|doi-access=free}}</ref>}} There is also an effort to recognize each Indigenous group as a distinct nation, much as there are distinct European, African, and Asian cultures in their respective places.<ref>{{cite web|title=University Of Guelph Brand Guide {{!}} Indigenous Peoples|url=https://guides.uoguelph.ca/guides/style-guide/inclusive-language/indigenous-peoples/|access-date=June 25, 2021|website=guides.uoguelph.ca|date=November 14, 2019 }}</ref>

''First Nations'' (most often used in the plural) has come into general use since the 1970s, replacing ''Indians'' and ''Indian bands'' in everyday vocabulary.<ref name="term" /><ref name="Terminology" /> However, on [[Indian reserve]]s, ''First Nations'' is being supplanted by members of various nations referring to themselves by their group or ethnic identity. In conversation, this would be "I am [[Haida people|Haida]]", or "we are [[Kwantlen First Nation|Kwantlens]]", in recognition of their First Nations ethnicities.<ref>{{cite book |title=Language and Identity |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wwvOjiqyU-EC&pg=PA1|first= John |last=Edwards |publisher= Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-69602-9 |year=2009 }}</ref> Also coming into general use since the 1970s, First Peoples refers to all Indigenous groups, i.e. First Nations, Inuit, and Métis.<ref name="FN">{{cite book|url=http://firstpeoplesofcanada.com/fp_treaties/john_fp33_indianact.html|title=The Indian Act of Canada – Origins: Legislation Concerning Canada's First Peoples |author=Elizabeth II |publisher=[[Assembly of First Nations]] |year=2004 |series=1 |place=Ottawa |page=3 |author-link=Elizabeth II |access-date=January 11, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/pr/pub/wf/trmrslt_e.asp?term=11 |title=Words First An Evolving Terminology Relating to Aboriginal Peoples in Canada |year=2004 |publisher=Communications Branch of Indian and Northern Affairs Canada |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030106124111/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/pr/pub/wf/trmrslt_e.asp?term=11 |archive-date=January 6, 2003 |access-date=May 24, 2020 }}</ref><ref name="indian">{{cite web |url=http://www.aidp.bc.ca/terminology_of_native_aboriginal_metis.pdf |title=Terminology of First Nations, Native, Aboriginal and Métis |year=2009 |publisher=Aboriginal Infant Development Programs of B.C. |access-date=June 26, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100714021655/http://www.aidp.bc.ca/terminology_of_native_aboriginal_metis.pdf |archive-date=July 14, 2010  }}</ref>

Notwithstanding Canada's location within the [[Americas]], the term ''Native American'' is hardly ever used in Canada, in order to avoid any confusion due to the ambiguous meaning of the word "American". Therefore, the term is typically used only in reference to the [[Native Americans in the United States|Indigenous peoples within the boundaries of the present-day United States]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Native American |url=http://oaadonline.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/dictionary/native-american |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121122035018/http://oaadonline.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/dictionary/native-american |archive-date=November 22, 2012 |access-date=May 27, 2013 |work=Oxford Advanced American Dictionary |quote=In Canada, the term Native American is not used, and the most usual way to refer to the Aboriginal peoples of Canada, other than the Inuit and Métis, is First Nations.}}</ref> ''Native Canadians'' was often used in Canada to differentiate this American term until the 1980s.<ref>{{cite web |website=firstpeoplesofcanada.com |title=Origins of Canada's First Peoples |url=http://firstpeoplesofcanada.com/fp_groups/fp_groups_origins.html |access-date=March 25, 2021}}</ref>

In contrast to the more-specific ''Aboriginal'', one of the issues with the term {{Wikt-lang|en|native|i=no}} is its general applicability: in certain contexts, it could be used in reference to non-Indigenous peoples in regards to an individual place of origin / birth.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |url=https://indigenousfoundations.arts.ubc.ca/terminology/#native |title=Terminology |website=Indigenous Foundations |publisher=First Nations & Indigenous Studies, [[University of British Columbia]] |year=2009}}</ref> For instance, people who were born or grew up in [[Calgary]] may call themselves "Calgary natives", as in they are ''native'' to that city. With this in mind, even the term ''native American'', as another example, may very well indicate someone who is ''native to America'' rather than a person who is ethnically Indigenous to the boundaries of the present-day United States. In this sense, ''native'' may encompass a broad range of populations and is therefore not recommended,<ref name=":1" /> although it is not generally considered offensive.

The ''[[Indian Act]]''&nbsp;(<abbr>[[Revised Statutes of Canada]] (R.S.C.)</abbr>, 1985, c. I-5) sets the legal term ''Indian'', designating that "a person who pursuant to this Act is registered as an Indian or is entitled to be registered as an Indian."<ref name="Branch">{{cite web|url=http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/i-5/|title=Consolidated federal laws of canada, Indian Act|last=Branch|first=Legislative Services|website=laws-lois.justice.gc.ca|language=en|access-date=October 4, 2017}}</ref> Section 5 of the act states that a registry shall be maintained "in which shall be recorded the name of every person who is entitled to be registered as an Indian under this Act."<ref name="Branch" /> No other term is legally recognized for the purpose of registration and the term ''Indian'' specifically excludes reference to Inuit as per section 4 of the act.<ref name="u408">{{cite web | title=The Indian Act | website=The Canadian Encyclopedia | date=Jun 6, 1944 | url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/timeline/the-indian-act | access-date=Nov 20, 2024}}</ref>

[[File:Aboriginal Community in Northern Ontario.JPG|thumb|An Aboriginal community in [[Northern Ontario]]]]

The term ''[[Eskimo]]'' has [[pejorative]] connotations in Canada and [[Greenland]]. Indigenous peoples in those areas have replaced the term ''Eskimo'' with ''Inuit'',<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hirschfelder| first1 = Arlene B|last2=Beamer|first2=Yvonne| title = Native Americans today: resources and activities for educators, grades 4–8| publisher = Teacher Ideas Press, 2000| year = 2002|page=3| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=p5SnvwKV5m8C&q=%22Inuit+or+Eskimo&pg=PA3| access-date =January 11, 2015|isbn=978-1-56308-694-6 }}
</ref><ref name=eski>{{cite web|url=http://www.expansionistparty.org/Eskimo.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071013174643/http://www.expansionistparty.org/Eskimo.html|archive-date=October 13, 2007|title="Eskimo" vs. "Inuit"|work=Expansionist Party of the United States | access-date =October 5, 2009 }}</ref> though the [[Yupik peoples|Yupik]] of [[Alaska]] and [[Siberia]] do not consider themselves Inuit, and [[Ethnography|ethnographers]] agree they are a distinct people.{{sfn|Olson|Pappas|1994|p=213}}<ref name=eski/> They prefer the terminology Yupik, Yupiit, or Eskimo. The [[Yupik languages]] are linguistically distinct from the [[Inuit languages]], but are related to each other.{{sfn|Olson|Pappas|1994|p=213}} [[Language family|Linguistic groups]] of [[Circumpolar peoples|Arctic people]] have no universal replacement term for ''Eskimo'', inclusive of all Inuit and Yupik across the geographical area inhabited by them.{{sfn|Olson|Pappas|1994|p=213}}

Besides these ethnic descriptors, Aboriginal peoples are often divided into legal categories based on their relationship with [[the Crown]] (i.e. the state). [[Constitution Act, 1867#First Nations, Inuit and Métis|Section 91(24)]] of the ''[[Constitution Act, 1867]]'' gives the federal government (as opposed to the provinces) the sole responsibility for "Indians, and Lands reserved for the Indians." The government inherited treaty obligations from the British colonial authorities in [[Eastern Canada]] and signed treaties itself with First Nations in [[Western Canada]] (the [[Numbered Treaties]]). The ''Indian Act'', passed by the federal Parliament in 1876, has long governed its interactions with all treaty and non-treaty peoples.<ref name="z557">{{cite web | title=Frequently Asked Questions | website=Indigenous Peoples Atlas of Canada | date=2018-06-08 | url=https://indigenouspeoplesatlasofcanada.ca/article/fn-frequently-asked-questions/ | access-date=2025-08-21}}</ref>

Members of First Nations bands who are subject to the ''Indian Act'' are compiled on a list called the [[Indian Register]], and such people are designated as status Indians. Many non-treaty First Nations and all Inuit and Métis are not subject to the ''Indian Act''. However, two court cases have clarified that Inuit, Métis, and [[Non-status Indian|non-status First Nations]] are all covered by the term ''Indians'' in the ''Constitution Act, 1867''. The first was ''[[Reference Re Eskimos]]'' (1939), covering Inuit; the second was ''[[Daniels v Canada (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)|Daniels v. Canada]]'' (2013), which concerns Métis and non-status First Nations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/court-rules-metis-non-status-indians-qualify-as-indians-under-act-1.1105186/ |title=Court rules Metis, non-status Indians qualify as 'Indians' under Act |date=January 8, 2013 |access-date=November 23, 2016|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130108152901/http://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/court-rules-metis-non-status-indians-qualify-as-indians-under-act-1.1105186 |archive-date=January 8, 2013  |publisher=CTV News}}</ref>

==History==
{{See also|History of Canada}}

===Paleo-Indian period===
{{See also|Peopling of the Americas|Paleo-Indians}}
{{Further|Technological and industrial history of Canada#The Stone Age: Fire (14,000 BC – AD 1600)}}
[[File:Early migrations mercator.svg|thumb|upright=1.6 |Map of [[early human migrations]] based on the [[Recent African origin of modern humans|Out of Africa theory]]; figures are in thousands of years ago (kya)<ref>{{cite book|first= Göran |last= Burenhult |title=Die ersten Menschen |publisher= Weltbild Verlag |year= 2000 |isbn= 978-3-8289-0741-6}}</ref>]]

According to [[List of archaeological periods (North America)|North American archaeological]] and genetic evidence, [[Peopling of the Americas|migration to North and South America]] made them the last continents in the world with [[early human migrations|human habitation]].<ref name="national">{{cite web|title=Atlas of the Human Journey-The Genographic Project|publisher=National Geographic Society.|date=1996–2008|url=https://genographic.nationalgeographic.com/genographic/atlas.html?era=e003|access-date=October 6, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110501094643/https://genographic.nationalgeographic.com/genographic/atlas.html?era=e003|archive-date=May 1, 2011}}</ref> During the [[Wisconsin glaciation]], 50,000–17,000 years ago, falling sea levels allowed people to move across the [[Beringia|Bering land bridge]] that joined Siberia to northwest North America (Alaska).<ref name=Goebel>{{cite journal |title=The Late Pleistocene Dispersal of Modern Humans in the Americas |url=http://www.centerfirstamericans.com/cfsa-publications/Science2008.pdf |year=2008 |doi=10.1126/science.1153569 |pmid=18339930 |volume=319 |issue=5869 |journal=Science |pages=1497–502 |vauthors=Goebel T, Waters MR, O'Rourke DH|bibcode=2008Sci...319.1497G |s2cid=36149744 }}
</ref> Alaska was [[Glacial refugium|ice-free]] because of [[Rain shadow|low snowfall]], allowing a [[small population size|small population]] to exist. The [[Laurentide ice sheet]] covered most of Canada, blocking [[nomad]]ic inhabitants and confining them to Alaska (East Beringia) for thousands of years.<ref>{{cite news |first=Nicholas |last=Wade |title=Pause Is Seen in a Continent's Peopling |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/13/science/linguistic-study-sheds-new-light-on-peopling-of-north-america.html?ref=science |date=March 13, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Pielou |first=E.C. |title=After the Ice Age: The Return of Life to Glaciated North America |publisher=[[University of Chicago Press]] |year=1991 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MO4QFKshlVcC&pg=PP1 |isbn=978-0-226-66812-3}}{{page needed|date=June 2016}}</ref>

[[Genetic history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Indigenous genetic studies]] suggest that the first inhabitants of the Americas share a single ancestral population, one that developed in isolation, conjectured to be Beringia.<ref name=SpencerWells2>{{cite book |first1=Spencer |last1=Wells |first2=Mark |last2=Read |title=The Journey of Man – A Genetic Odyssey |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WAsKm-_zu5sC&pg=PP1 |publisher=Random House |isbn=978-0-8129-7146-0 |year=2002 |pages=138–140}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=Cecil M. |last=Lewis |title=Hierarchical modeling of genome-wide Short Tandem Repeat (STR) markers infers native American prehistory |journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology |volume=141 |issue=2 |pages=281–289 |date=February 2010 |doi=10.1002/ajpa.21143 |pmid=19672848 |bibcode=2010AJPA..141..281L }}</ref> The isolation of these peoples in Beringia might have lasted 10,000–20,000 years.<ref>{{cite web |title=New World Settlers Took 20,000-Year Pit Stop |first=Ker |last=Than |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2008/02/080214-america-layover.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080219013512/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2008/02/080214-america-layover.html |archive-date=February 19, 2008 |publisher=National Geographic Society |year=2008 |access-date=January 23, 2010}}</ref><ref name="nda">{{cite journal |first1=Sigrún |last1=Sigurðardóttir |first2=Agnar |last2=Helgason |first3=Jeffrey R. |last3=Gulcher |first4=Kári |last4=Stefansson |first5=Peter |last5=Donnelly |title=The Mutation Rate in the Human mtDNA Control Region |journal=American Journal of Human Genetics |volume=66 |date=May 2000 |pmid=10756141 |issue=5 |pages=1599–1609 |pmc=1378010 |doi=10.1086/302902 |bibcode=2000AmJHG..66.1599S }}
</ref><ref name=discov>{{cite web|title=First Americans Endured 20,000-Year Layover – Jennifer Viegas, Discovery News |url=http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2008/02/13/beringia-native-american.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080214210946/http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2008/02/13/beringia-native-american.html |archive-date=February 14, 2008 |access-date=November 18, 2009 |quote=Archaeological evidence, in fact, recognizes that people started to leave Beringia for the New World around 40,000 years ago, but rapid expansion into North America didn't occur until about 15,000 years ago, when the ice had literally broken}} [http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2008/02/13/beringia-native-american-02.html page 2] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120313061401/http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2008/02/13/beringia-native-american-02.html |date=March 13, 2012 }}</ref> Around 16,500 years ago, the [[Last Glacial Maximum|glaciers began melting]], allowing people to move south and east into Canada and beyond.<ref name="aaa">{{cite journal |last1=Tamm |first1=Erika |first2=Toomas |last2=Kivisild |first3=Maere |last3=Reidla |display-authors=etal |title=Beringian Standstill and Spread of Native American Founders |journal=[[PLoS ONE]] |volume=2 |date=September 5, 2007 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0000829 |pmid=17786201 |issue=9 |pages=e829 |pmc=1952074|bibcode=2007PLoSO...2..829T |doi-access=free }}
</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Dyke |first1=A.S. |first2=A. |last2=Moore |first3=L. |last3=Robertson |year=2003 |url=http://geopub.nrcan.gc.ca/moreinfo_e.php?id=214399 |title=Deglaciation of North America |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120216073131/http://geopub.nrcan.gc.ca/moreinfo_e.php?id=214399 |archive-date=February 16, 2012 |work=Geological Survey of Canada Open File, 1574}} (Thirty-two digital maps at 1:7 000 000 scale with accompanying digital chronological database and one poster (two sheets) with full map series.</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=David K |last=Jordan |title=Prehistoric Beringia |url=http://www.anthro.ucsd.edu/~dkjordan/arch/beringia.html |publisher=University of California-San Diego |year=2009 |access-date=April 15, 2010 |archive-date=February 12, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140212155854/http://www.anthro.ucsd.edu/~dkjordan/arch/beringia.html }}</ref>

The first inhabitants of North America arrived in Canada at least 14,000 years ago.<ref name="FaganDurrani2016"/> It is believed the inhabitants entered the Americas pursuing [[Pleistocene]] mammals such as the [[Castoroides|giant beaver]], [[Steppe bison|steppe wisent]] (bison), [[muskox]], [[mastodon]]s, [[woolly mammoth]]s and ancient reindeer (early caribou).<ref name="Meltzer">{{cite book |last=Meltzer |first=David J. |title=First Peoples in a New World: Colonizing Ice Age America |chapter=Chapter 2: The Landscape of Colonization: Glaciers, Climates, and the Environments of Ice Age North America |publisher=University of California Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-520-25052-9}}</ref> One route hypothesized is that people walked south by way of an ice-free corridor on the east side of the [[Rocky Mountains]], and then fanned out across North America before continuing on to South America.<ref name="albert">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dZYGdbWTXesC&pg=PA6 |title=American environmental history: an introduction |first=Carolyn |last=Merchant |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-231-14034-8 |page=6}}</ref> The other conjectured route is that they migrated, either on foot or using [[boat#History|primitive boats]], down the Pacific coast to the tip of South America, and then crossed the Rockies and [[Andes]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=K. R. |last=Fladmark |title=Alternate Migration Corridors for Early Man in North America |journal=American Antiquity |jstor=279189 |date=January 1979 |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=55–69 |doi=10.2307/279189|s2cid=162243347 }}</ref> Evidence of the latter has been covered by a [[sea level rise]] of hundreds of metres following the last ice age.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.realclimate.org/index.php/archives/2009/01/sea-will-rise-to-levels-of-last-ice-age/ |title=68 Responses to Sea will rise 'to levels of last Ice Age' |date=January 26, 2009 |via=realclimate.org |publisher=Center for Climate Systems Research, Columbia University |access-date=October 6, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091027133849/http://www.realclimate.org/index.php/archives/2009/01/sea-will-rise-to-levels-of-last-ice-age/ |archive-date=October 27, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Harris |first1=Ann G. |last2=Tuttle |first2=Esther |last3=Tuttle |first3=Sherwood D. |title=Geology of National Parks |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xr7v7GNmHs0C&pg=PP1 |year=2004 |publisher=Kendall/Hunt Publishing Company |isbn=978-0-7872-9970-5 |pages=1–}}</ref>

The [[Old Crow Flats]] and basin was one of the areas in Canada untouched by glaciations during the [[Quaternary glaciation|Pleistocene Ice ages]], thus it served as a pathway and refuge for ice age plants and animals.<ref name="mountain">{{cite web |title=Life in Crow Flats-Part 1 |work=Old Crow's official Website |publisher=Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation |date=1998–2009 |url=http://www.oldcrow.ca/cf1.htm |access-date=September 18, 2009}}</ref> The area holds evidence of early human habitation in Canada dating from about 12,000 years ago.<ref name="CordellLightfoot2008">{{cite book |first1=Linda S. |last1=Cordell |first2=Kent |last2=Lightfoot |first3=Francis |last3=McManamon |first4=George |last4=Milner |title=Archaeology in America: An Encyclopedia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=arfWRW5OFVgC&pg=PA3-PA249 |volume=4 |year=2008 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=978-0-313-02189-3 |page=3}}</ref> Fossils from the area include some never accounted for in North America, such as [[hyena]]s and large [[camel]]s.<ref name="taiga.net">{{cite web |url=http://www.taiga.net/wetlands/oldcrow/oc_gen.html |title=Old Crow Flats |publisher=taiga.net |access-date=August 5, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070823023629/http://www.taiga.net/wetlands/oldcrow/oc_gen.html |archive-date=August 23, 2007  }}</ref> [[Bluefish Caves]] is an archaeological site in [[Yukon]] from which a specimen of apparently human-worked mammoth bone was radiocarbon dated to 12,000 years ago.<ref name="CordellLightfoot2008"/>

[[File:Clovis Point.jpg|thumb|left|upright|alt=A Clovis blade with medium to large lanceolate spear-knifepoints. Side is parallel to convex and exhibit careful pressure flaking along the blade edge. The broadest area is near the midsection or toward the base. The Base is distinctly concave with a characteristic flute or channel flake removed from one or, more commonly, both surfaces of the blade. The lower edges of the blade and base is ground to dull edges for hafting. Clovis points also tend to be thicker than the typically thin latter stage Folsom points. Length: 4–20 cm/1.5–8 in. Width: 2.5–5 cm/1–2 | A [[Clovis point]] created using [[Lithic reduction|bi-facial percussion flaking]] (that is, each face is flaked on both edges alternatively with a percussor)]]
Clovis sites dated at 13,500 years ago were discovered in western North America during the 1930s. [[Clovis culture|Clovis peoples]] were regarded as the first widespread [[Paleo-Indians|Paleo-Indian]] inhabitants of the [[New World]] and ancestors to all [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Indigenous peoples in the Americas]].<ref name="cloves">{{cite book |title=Ice Age People of North America |last=Lepper |first=Bradley T. |editor-last1=Bonnichsen |editor-first1=Robson |editor-last2=Turnmire |editor-first2=Karen |year=1999 |publisher=Oregon State University Press |location=Corvallis |isbn=978-0-87071-458-0 |pages=362–394 |chapter=Pleistocene Peoples of Midcontinental North America |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0mNuAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP1}}</ref> 

Localized regional cultures developed from the time of the [[Younger Dryas]] cold climate period from 12,900 to 11,500 years ago.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kennett |first1=D.J. |last2=Kennett |first2=J.P. |last3=West |first3=A. |display-authors=etal |title=Nanodiamonds in the Younger Dryas boundary sediment layer |journal=Science |volume=323 |issue=5910 |page=94 |date=January 2009 |pmid=19119227 |doi=10.1126/science.1162819|bibcode=2009Sci...323...94K |s2cid=206514910 |url=http://doc.rero.ch/record/16088/files/PAL_E3879.pdf }}</ref> The [[Folsom tradition]] is characterized by the use of [[Folsom point]]s as projectile tips at archaeological sites. These tools assisted activities at kill sites that marked the slaughter and butchering of bison.<ref>{{cite book|last=Hillerman|first=Tony |chapter=The Hunt for the Lost American|title=The Great Taos Bank Robbery: And Other Indian Country Affairs|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nYCEz1UrFFEC&pg=PA52|date=June 1980|publisher=University of New Mexico Press|isbn=978-0-8263-0530-5|page=52}}
</ref>

The land bridge existed until 13,000–11,000 years ago, long after the oldest proven human settlements in the New World began.<ref name=mapSurvey>{{cite journal |last1=Dyke |first1=Arthur S. |last2=Prest |first2=Victor K. |title=Late Wisconsinan and Holocene History of the Laurentide Ice Sheet |journal=Géographie Physique et Quaternaire |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=237–263 |date=1987 |doi=10.7202/032681ar |url=https://www.erudit.org/revue/gpq/1987/v41/n2/032681ar.pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref> Lower sea levels in the [[Queen Charlotte Sound (Canada)|Queen Charlotte sound]] and [[Hecate Strait]] produced great grass lands called ''archipelago of [[Haida Gwaii]]''.<ref name="hadi">{{cite web |title=Prehistory of Haida Gwaii |work=Civilization.ca-Haida-The people and the land-Prehistory |publisher=Canadian Museum of Civilization Corporation |date=June 8, 2001 |url=http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/aborig/haida/happr01e.shtml}}</ref>
[[Hunter-gatherer]]s of the area left distinctive [[lithic technology]] tools and the remains of large butchered mammals, occupying the area from 13,000–[[7th millennium BC|9,000 years ago]].<ref name="hadi"/> In July 1992, the Government of Canada officially designated [[X̱á:ytem]] (near [[Mission, British Columbia]]) as a [[National Historic Sites of Canada|national historic site]], one of the first Indigenous spiritual sites in Canada to be formally recognized in this manner.{{sfn|Jameson|1997|p=159}}

The [[Plano cultures]] was a group of hunter-gatherer communities that occupied the Great Plains area of North America between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago.<ref name="palo">{{cite web|last1=Reynolds |first1=Graham |first2=Richard |last2=MacKinnon |first3=Ken |last3=MacDonald |publisher=Folkus Atlantic Productions |title=Period 1 (10,000–8,000 years ago) Palaeo-Indian culture |work=Learners Portal |url=http://www.learnersportal.com/CanadaFP/Ancient/per1.html |access-date=September 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110713193402/http://www.learnersportal.com/CanadaFP/Ancient/per1.html |archive-date=July 13, 2011 }}</ref> The Paleo-Indians moved into new territory as it emerged from under the glaciers. Big game flourished in this new environment.{{sfn|Taylor|2002|p=10}} The Plano culture is characterized by a range of projectile point tools collectively called [[Plano point]]s, which were used to hunt [[bison]]. Their diets also included [[pronghorn]], [[elk]], [[deer]], [[raccoon]] and [[coyote]].<ref name="palo"/> At the beginning of the [[Archaic period (North America)|Archaic period]], they began to adopt a [[Sedentary lifestyle|sedentary]] approach to subsistence.<ref name="palo"/> Sites in and around [[Belmont, Colchester, Nova Scotia|Belmont, Nova Scotia]], have evidence of Plano-Indians, indicating small seasonal hunting camps, perhaps re-visited over generations from around 11,000–10,000 years ago.<ref name="palo"/> Seasonal large and smaller game fish and fowl were food and raw material sources. Adaptation to the harsh environment included tailored clothing and skin-covered tents on wooden frames.<ref name="palo"/>

===Archaic period===
{{See also|Pre-Columbian era}}

The North American climate stabilized by 8000&nbsp;[[Common Era|BCE]] (10,000 years ago); climatic conditions were very similar to today's.<ref name="icaage"/> This led to widespread migration, [[Plant cultivation|cultivation]] and later a dramatic rise in population all over the Americas.<ref name="icaage"/> Over the course of thousands of years, Indigenous peoples of the Americas domesticated, bred and cultivated a large array of plant species. These species now constitute 50–60% of all crops in cultivation worldwide.<ref>{{cite book |title=Foreign agriculture |volume=24 |year=1962 |publisher=Bureau of Agricultural Economics |location=United States, Foreign Agricultural Service |page=167}}{{isbn|978-0-16-038463-9}}
<!--ISBNs weren't issued until 1965 so I'm putting this outside the ref to stop the cs1 error it's throwing--></ref>

[[File:Na-Dene langs.png|thumb|alt="Map of North America showing in red the pre-contact distribution of Na-Dene languages"|Distribution of [[Na-Dene languages]] shown in red]]

The vastness and variety of Canada's climates, ecology, vegetation, [[fauna]], and landform separations have defined ancient peoples implicitly into cultural or [[Linguistics|linguistic]] divisions. Canada is surrounded north, east, and west with coastline and since the last ice age, Canada has consisted of distinct forest regions. Language contributes to the identity of a people by influencing social life ways and spiritual practices.<ref name="prepre"/> Indigenous religions developed from [[anthropomorphism]] and [[animism]] philosophies.<ref>{{cite book |last=Friesen |first=John |title=Rediscovering the First Nations of Canada. |year=1997 |publisher=Detselig Enterprises Ltd |location=Calgary, AB |isbn=978-1-55059-143-9}}
</ref>

The placement of artifacts and materials within an Archaic burial site indicated social differentiation based upon status.<ref name="icaage"/> There is a continuous record of occupation of [[Stó꞉lō|S'ólh Téméxw]] by Indigenous people dating from the early [[Holocene]] period, 10,000–9,000 years ago.<ref name="thor">{{cite book |title=You Are Asked to Witness: The Stó:lō in Canada's Pacific Coast History |year=1997 |publisher=((Stó:lō Heritage Trust))|location=Chilliwack, BC |isbn=978-0-9681577-0-1 |editor=Carlson, Keith Thor}}</ref> Archaeological sites at [[Stave Lake]], [[Coquitlam Lake]], [[Fort Langley]] and region uncovered early period artifacts. These early inhabitants were highly mobile hunter-gatherers, consisting of about 20 to 50 members of an extended family.<ref name="thor"/>{{verify source | reason=Removed another citation for this sentence to a personal website; not sure if remaining citation verifies the information in the sentence on its own. | date=March 2014}} The [[Na-Dene languages|Na-Dene]] people occupied much of the land area of northwest and central North America starting around 8,000&nbsp;BCE.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.historyandtheheadlines.abc-clio.com/ContentPages/ContentPage.aspx?entryId=1171754&currentSection=1161468&productid=5 |title=American Indian Heritage Month: Commemoration vs. Exploitation |work=ABC-CLIO |access-date=October 2, 2009}}</ref> They were the earliest ancestors of the [[Athabaskan languages|Athabaskan]]-speaking peoples, including the [[Navajo]] and [[Apache]]. They had villages with large multi-family dwellings, used seasonally during the summer, from which they hunted, fished and gathered food supplies for the winter.<ref>{{cite book |last=Leer |first=Jeff |author2=Doug Hitch |author3=John Ritter |title=Interior Tlingit noun dictionary: The dialects spoken by Tlingit elders of Carcross and Teslin, Yukon, and Atlin, British Columbia |year=2001 |publisher=Yukon Native Language Centre |location=Whitehorse, Yukon Territory |isbn=978-1-55242-227-4}}
</ref> The [[Wyandot people|Wendat]] peoples settled into [[Southern Ontario]] along the [[Eramosa River]] around 8,000–7,000&nbsp;BCE (10,000–9,000&nbsp;years ago).{{sfn|Ray|1996|p=}} They were concentrated between [[Lake Simcoe]] and [[Georgian Bay]]. Wendat hunted caribou to survive on the glacier-covered land.{{sfn|Ray|1996|p=}} Many different First Nations cultures relied upon the buffalo starting by 6,000–5,000&nbsp;BCE (8,000–7,000&nbsp;years ago).{{sfn|Ray|1996|p=}} They hunted buffalo by herding migrating buffalo off cliffs. [[Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump]], near [[Fort Macleod]], Alberta, is a hunting grounds that was in use for about 5,000 years.{{sfn|Ray|1996|p=}}

[[File:Cambridge Bay Thule Site 1998-06-28.jpg|thumb|left|alt=Photograph of a circular arrangement of rocks on open ground with a body of water in the background|[[Thule people|Thule]] site ([[Copper Inuit]]) near the waters of [[Cambridge Bay]] ([[Victoria Island]])]]

By 7,000–5000&nbsp;BCE (9,000–7,000&nbsp;years ago) the [[British Columbia Coast|west coast of Canada]] saw various cultures who organized themselves around salmon fishing.{{sfn|Ray|1996|p=}} The [[Nuu-chah-nulth]] of [[Vancouver Island]] began [[whaling]] with advanced long spears at about this time.{{sfn|Ray|1996|p=}} The [[Maritime Archaic]] is one group of North America's [[Archaic Period (Americas)|Archaic]] culture of [[Marine mammal|sea-mammal]] hunters in the [[subarctic]]. They prospered from approximately 7,000&nbsp;BCE–1,500&nbsp;BCE (9,000–3,500 years ago) along the [[Arctic Ocean|Atlantic Coast]] of North America.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.therooms.ca/museum/mnotes12.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060510135435/http://www.therooms.ca/museum/mnotes12.asp |archive-date=May 10, 2006 |title=Museum Notes-The Maritime Archaic Tradition |work=By James A. Tuck-The Rooms Provincial Art Gallery |access-date=October 5, 2009}}</ref> Their settlements included [[longhouse]]s and boat-topped temporary or seasonal houses. They engaged in long-distance trade, using as currency white [[chert]], a rock quarried from northern [[Labrador]] to [[Maine]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Tuck |first=J. A. |title=The excavation of an Archaic Indian Cemetery in Newfoundland. Newfoundland Social and Economic Studies 17 |year=1976 |publisher=Institute of Social and Economic Research |location=St. John's |chapter=Ancient peoples of Port au Choix |isbn=978-0-919666-12-2}}</ref> The [[Pre-Columbian era|Pre-Columbian]] culture, whose members were called [[Red Paint People]], is indigenous to the [[New England]] and [[Atlantic Canada]] regions of North America. The culture flourished between 3,000&nbsp;BCE&nbsp;– 1,000&nbsp;BCE (5,000–3,000&nbsp;years ago) and was named after their burial ceremonies, which used large quantities of red [[ochre]] to cover bodies and grave goods.<ref>{{cite web |title=The so-called "Red Paint People |access-date=October 18, 2009 |year=1997 |publisher=University of Maine |work=Brian Robinson |url=http://www.seacoastnh.com/history/prehistoric/redpaint.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100114031021/http://www.seacoastnh.com/history/prehistoric/redpaint.html |archive-date=January 14, 2010  }}</ref>

The [[Arctic small tool tradition]] is a broad cultural entity that developed along the [[Alaska Peninsula]], around [[Bristol Bay]], and on the eastern shores of the Bering Strait around 2,500&nbsp;BCE (4,500&nbsp;years ago).<ref name="Fagan"/> These [[Paleo-Arctic tradition|Paleo-Arctic]] peoples had a highly distinctive toolkit of small blades ([[Microblade technology|microblades]]) that were pointed at both ends and used as side- or end-barbs on [[arrow]]s or spears made of other materials, such as bone or [[antler]]. [[Scraper (archaeology)|Scrapers]], engraving tools and [[adze]] blades were also included in their toolkits.<ref name="Fagan"/> The Arctic small tool tradition branches off into two cultural variants, including the Pre-Dorset, and the [[Independence II culture|Independence traditions]], ancestors of the [[Thule people]], and Inuit displaced these two groups by 1000&nbsp;CE.<ref name="Fagan"/>{{rp|179–81}}
{{Clear}}

===Post-Archaic periods===
{{See also|List of archaeological periods (North America)}}

| width=200
| imageleft=-150
|height=100

|image-width=200
| alt=A northerly section focusing on the Saugeen, Laurel and Point Peninsula complexes of the map showing south eastern United States and the Great Lakes area of Canada showing the Hopewell Interaction Sphere and in different colours the various local expressions of the Hopewell cultures, including the Laurel complex, Saugeen complex, Point Peninsula complex, Marksville culture, Copena culture, Kansas City Hopewell, Swift Creek culture, Goodall focus, Crab Orchard culture and Havana Hopewell culture.
