The [[Old Copper complex]] societies dating from 3,000&nbsp;BCE&nbsp;– 500&nbsp;BCE (5,000–2,500&nbsp;years ago) are a manifestation of the [[Woodland period|Woodland culture]], and are pre-pottery in nature.{{sfn|Winchell|1881|pp=601–602}} Evidence found in the northern [[Great Lakes]] regions indicates that they extracted copper from local glacial deposits and used it in its [[Native copper|natural form]] to manufacture tools and implements.{{sfn|Winchell|1881|pp=601–602}}

The Woodland cultural period dates from about 1,000&nbsp;BCE&nbsp;– 1,000&nbsp;CE, and has locales in [[Ontario]], [[Quebec]], and [[The Maritimes|Maritime]] regions.<ref>{{cite web|title=C. Prehistoric Periods (Eras of Adaptation) |publisher=The University of Calgary (The Applied History Research Group) |year=2000 |url=https://www.ucalgary.ca/applied_history/tutor/firstnations/periods.html |access-date=April 15, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100412205024/http://www.ucalgary.ca/applied_history/tutor/firstnations/periods.html |archive-date=April 12, 2010  }}</ref> The introduction of pottery distinguishes the Woodland culture from the earlier Archaic stage inhabitants. [[Laurentides|Laurentian]] people of southern Ontario manufactured the oldest pottery excavated to date in Canada.<ref name="prepre"/> They created pointed-bottom beakers decorated by a cord marking technique that involved impressing tooth implements into wet clay. Woodland technology included items such as beaver incisor knives, bangles, and chisels. The population practising sedentary agricultural life ways continued to increase on a diet of squash, corn, and bean crops.<ref name="prepre">{{cite book |last=Fagan |first=Brian M. |others=University of California |title=People of the Earth: An Introduction to World Prehistory |year=1992 |publisher=[[HarperCollins|Harper Collins]] |isbn=978-0-321-01457-3 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/peopleofearthint09edfaga }}
</ref>

The Hopewell tradition is an Indigenous  culture that flourished along American rivers from 300&nbsp;BCE&nbsp;– 500&nbsp;CE. At its greatest extent, the [[Hopewell tradition|Hopewell Exchange System]] networked cultures and societies with the peoples on the Canadian shores of [[Lake Ontario]]. Canadian expression of the Hopewellian peoples encompasses the [[Point Peninsula complex|Point Peninsula]], [[Saugeen complex|Saugeen]], and [[Laurel complex]]es.<ref>{{cite web |title=A History of the Native People of Canada |work=Dr. James V. Wright |publisher=[[Canadian Museum of Civilization]] |year=2009 |url=http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/archeo/hnpc/npvol25e.shtml |access-date=October 9, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Ohio Historical Society |url=http://www.ohiohistorycentral.org/entry.php?rec=1283 |title=Hopewell Culture-Ohio History Central-A product of the Ohio Historical Society |publisher=Hopewell-Ohio History Central |year=2009 |access-date=September 18, 2009}}</ref><ref name="Price">{{cite book |first1=Douglas T. |last1=Price |first2=Gary M. |last2=Feinman |year=2008 |title=Images of the Past, 5th edition |pages=[https://archive.org/details/imagesofpast0005pric/page/274 274–277] |location=New York |publisher=McGraw-Hill |isbn=978-0-07-340520-9 |url=https://archive.org/details/imagesofpast0005pric/page/274 }}</ref>

====First Nations====
{{Main|First Nations in Canada}}

[[File:Chief George and daughter.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=Black and white photograph of Skwxwu7mesh Chief George from the village of Senakw with his daughter in traditional regalia.|Chief George from the village of [[Senakw]] with his daughter in traditional [[regalia]], {{circa|1906}}]]

First Nations peoples had settled and established trade routes across what is now Canada by 500&nbsp;BCE&nbsp;– 1,000&nbsp;CE. Communities developed each with its own culture, customs, and character.<ref name="Joe">{{cite book |last1=Joe |first1=Rita |first2=Lesley |last2=Choyce |title=The Native Canadian Anthology |year=2005 |publisher=Nimbus Publishing (CN) |isbn=978-1-895900-04-0}}</ref> In the northwest are the [[Athabaskan languages|Athapaskan speaking]], [[Slavey]], [[Tłı̨chǫ]], [[Northern Tutchone|Tutchone]], and [[Tlingit]]. Along the Pacific coast are the [[Tsimshian]]; Haida; [[Coast Salish]]; [[Kwakwakaʼwakw]]; [[Heiltsuk]]; [[Nuu-chah-nulth|Nootka]]; [[Nisga'a]]; [[Senakw]] and [[Gitxsan]]. In the Plains are the [[Blackfoot Confederacy|Niisitapi]]; [[Kainai Nation|Káínawa]]; [[Tsuutʼina Nation|Tsuutʼina]]; and [[Piikani Nation|Piikáni]]. In the Northern Woodlands are the [[Cree]] and [[Chipewyan]]. Around the Great Lakes are the [[Anishinaabe]]; [[Algonquin people|Algonquin]]; [[Haudenosaunee]] and Wendat. Along the Atlantic Coast are the [[Wolastoqiyik]], [[Innu]], [[Abenaki]], and [[Mi'kmaq]] and formerly the [[Beothuk]].{{citation needed|date=November 2024}}

Many First Nations civilizations<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/english/civilization |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120718042505/http://oxforddictionaries.com/definition/english/civilization |archive-date=July 18, 2012 |title=civilization – definition of civilization in English from the Oxford dictionary |publisher=Oxforddictionaries.com |access-date=October 25, 2015}}</ref> established characteristics and hallmarks that included permanent urban settlements or cities,<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Prine |first=Elizabeth |url=https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/1357826/Native-American |title=Native American &#124; indigenous peoples of Canada and United States |encyclopedia=Britannica.com |date=April 17, 2015 |access-date=October 25, 2015}}</ref> agriculture, civic and [[Mound Builders|monumental architecture]], and [[complex society|complex societal hierarchies]].<ref name="complex"/> These cultures had evolved and changed by the time of the first permanent European arrivals ({{Circa|late 15th}}–early 16th centuries), and have been brought forward through archaeological investigations.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Willey |first1=Gordon R |first2=Philip |last2=Phillips |title=Method and Theory in American Archaeology |access-date=October 18, 2009 |year=1957 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |pages=1(introduction) |url=https://www.questia.com/PM.qst?a=o&d=6136197 |archive-date=June 28, 2012 |via=[[Questia]] |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120628025551/http://www.questia.com/PM.qst?a=o&d=6136197 }} {{isbn|978-0-226-89888-9}}</ref>

There are indications of contact made before [[Christopher Columbus]] between the first peoples and those from other continents. Indigenous people in Canada first interacted with Europeans around 1000 CE, but prolonged contact came after Europeans established permanent settlements in the 17th and 18th centuries.<ref name="Woodcock, part I"/> European written accounts generally recorded friendliness of the First Nations, who profited in trade with Europeans.<ref name="Woodcock, part I"/> Such trade generally strengthened the more organized political entities such as the [[Iroquois|Iroquois Confederation]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Eric |last=Wolf |title=Europe and the People Without History |access-date=October 6, 2009 |date=December 3, 1982 |publisher=University of California Press; 1 edition |isbn=978-0-520-04898-0 |chapter-url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/40564/Eric-Wolf-Europe-and-the-People-Without-History-introduction |chapter=Chapter 6 |author-link=Eric Wolf |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/europepeoplewit008258 }} URL gives introduction online</ref> Throughout the 16th century, European fleets made almost annual visits to the eastern shores of Canada to cultivate the fishing opportunities. A sideline industry emerged in the un-organized [[Fur trade|traffic of furs]] overseen by the [[British Indian Department]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oHlLvzRZ-1sC&pg=PP1 |title=A Narrow Vision: Duncan Campbell Scott and the Administration of Indian Affairs in Canada |first=E. Brian |last=Titley |location=Vancouver |publisher=University Of British Columbia Press |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-7748-0420-2}}</ref>

Prominent First Nations people include Joe Capilano, who met with King of the United Kingdom, [[Edward VII]], to speak of the need to settle [[land claim]]s and [[Ovide Mercredi]], a leader at both the [[Meech Lake Accord]] constitutional reform discussions and [[Oka Crisis]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Ovide Mercredi installed as chancellor of Manitoba's newest university |publisher=[[CBC News]] |date=November 7, 2007 |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/ovide-mercredi-installed-as-chancellor-of-manitoba-s-newest-university-1.683199 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071109143107/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/ovide-mercredi-installed-as-chancellor-of-manitoba-s-newest-university-1.683199 |archive-date=November 9, 2007 |access-date=October 3, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The History of Metropolitan Vancouver's Hall of Fame Joe Capilano |url=http://www.vancouverhistory.ca/whoswho_C.htm |access-date=October 5, 2009 |archive-date=May 3, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090503033211/http://www.vancouverhistory.ca/whoswho_C.htm }}</ref>

====Inuit====
{{Main|Inuit}}

[[Inuit]] are the descendants of what [[Anthropology|anthropologists]] call the [[Thule people|Thule culture]], which emerged from western Alaska around 1,000&nbsp;CE and spread eastward across the [[Arctic]], displacing the [[Dorset culture]] (in [[Inuktitut]], the ''Tuniit''). Inuit historically referred to the Tuniit as "giants", who were taller and stronger than the Inuit.<ref>{{cite web |last=Rigby |first=Bruce |title=101. Qaummaarviit Historic Park, Nunavut Handbook |url=http://www.nunavuthandbook.com/parks_pgs_297_331.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060529123547/http://www.nunavuthandbook.com/parks_pgs_297_331.pdf |archive-date=May 29, 2006 |access-date=October 2, 2009}}</ref> Researchers hypothesize that the Dorset culture lacked dogs, larger weapons and other technologies used by the expanding Inuit society.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.historysociety.ca/content/en/pdfs/Jamieson2.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071030193732/http://www.historysociety.ca/content/en/pdfs/Jamieson2.pdf |archive-date=October 30, 2007 |title=The Dorsets: Depicting Culture Through Soapstone Carving |website=historysociety.ca |access-date=October 5, 2009}}</ref> By 1300, Inuit had settled in west Greenland, and finally moved into east Greenland over the following century. The Inuit had trade routes with more southern cultures. Boundary disputes were common and led to aggressive actions.<ref name=warin>{{cite web |url=http://www.heritage.nf.ca/aboriginal/innu_culture.html |title=Innu Culture 3. Innu-Inuit 'Warfare' |year=1999 |publisher=Adrian Tanner Department of Anthropology-Memorial University of Newfoundland |access-date=October 5, 2009 |archive-date=August 23, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110823015544/http://www.heritage.nf.ca/aboriginal/innu_culture.html }}</ref>

[[File:Inuit hunter with harpoon.jpg|thumb|left|alt="black and white image of an Inuit hunter seated in a kayak holding a harpoon"|[[Inuit|Inuk]] in a [[kayak]], {{circa|1908–1914}}]]

Warfare was common among Inuit groups with sufficient population density. Inuit, such as the [[Nunamiut]] ([[Uummarmiut]]) who inhabited the [[Mackenzie River]] delta area, often engaged in common warfare. The Central Arctic Inuit lacked the population density to engage in warfare. In the 13th century, the Thule culture began arriving in Greenland from what is now Canada. Norse accounts are scant. Norse-made items from Inuit campsites in Greenland were obtained by either trade or plunder.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.heritage.nf.ca/aboriginal/inuit_history.html |title=Inuit Post-Contact History |publisher=Memorial University of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. |access-date=October 5, 2009 |archive-date=December 18, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081218132650/http://www.heritage.nf.ca/aboriginal/inuit_history.html }}</ref> One account, [[Ívar Bárðarson]], speaks of "small people" with whom the Norsemen fought.<ref>{{cite book |first=Hans Christian |last=Gulløv |title=Grønlands Forhistorie |year=2005 |isbn=978-87-02-01724-3 |page=17|publisher=Gyldendal A/S }}</ref> 14th-century accounts relate that a western settlement, one of the two Norse settlements, was taken over by the [[Skræling]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Fitzhugh |first=William W. |editor1-last=Fitzhugh |editor1-first=William W. |editor2-first=Elisabeth I. |editor2-last=Ward |title=Vikings: The North Atlantic Saga |year=2000 |publisher=[[Smithsonian Institution]] |location=Washington, D.C. |isbn=978-1-56098-995-0 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/vikingsnorthatla00fitz/page/193 193–205]|title-link=Atlantic Ocean }}
</ref>

After the disappearance of the Norse colonies in Greenland, the Inuit had no contact with Europeans for at least a century. By the mid-16th century, [[Basques|Basque]] fishers were already working the Labrador coast and had established whaling stations on land, such as those excavated at [[Red Bay, Newfoundland and Labrador|Red Bay]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=McGhee |first=Robert |title=Northern Approaches. Before Columbus: Early European Visitors to the New World |journal=The Beaver. Exploring Canada's History |date=June–July 1992 |volume=3 |page=194 |issn=0005-7517}}</ref> The Inuit appear not to have interfered with their operations, but they did raid the stations in winter for tools, and particularly worked iron, which they adapted to native needs.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kleivan |first=H |title=The Eskimos of Northeast Labrador |publisher=Norsk Polarinstitutt Skrifter |year=1966 |volume=139 |page=9 |oclc=786916953}}
</ref>

Notable among the Inuit are [[Abraham Ulrikab]] and family who became a [[zoo]] exhibit in [[Hamburg]], Germany, and [[Tanya Tagaq]], a traditional [[Inuit throat singing|throat singer]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Minogue |first=Sarah |title=When Inuit become zoo curiosities "We sat there like pieces of art in a showcase on display" |website=Nunatsiaq News |date=September 23, 2005 |url=http://www.nunatsiaq.com/archives/50923/news/features/50923_01.html |access-date=October 6, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090917185643/http://www.nunatsiaq.com/archives/50923/news/features/50923_01.html |archive-date=September 17, 2009  }}</ref> [[Abe Okpik]] was instrumental in helping Inuit obtain [[surname]]s rather than [[disc number]]s and [[Kiviaq]] (David Ward) won the legal right to use his single-word [[Inuktitut]] name.<ref>{{cite web|title=Kiviaq versus Canada film by Zacharias Kunuk Produced by Katarina Soukup |publisher=Isuma Distribution International Inc. |year=2006 |url=http://www.canadacouncil.ca/NR/rdonlyres/97B12343-AC79-4ED6-AC1E-055350618B16/0/InuitFactSheetEN.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101214163906/http://www.canadacouncil.ca/NR/rdonlyres/97B12343-AC79-4ED6-AC1E-055350618B16/0/InuitFactSheetEN.pdf |archive-date=December 14, 2010 |access-date=October 3, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Hanson |first=Ann Meekitjuk |title=Nunavut 99-What's In A Name? Names, as well as events, mark the road to Nunavut |publisher=Nunavut.com |url=http://www.nunavut.com/nunavut99/english/name.html |access-date=October 3, 2009 |archive-date=November 7, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161107123650/http://www.nunavut.com/nunavut99/english/name.html }}</ref>

====Métis====
{{Main|Métis}}

[[File:Mixed blood Fur trader 1870.jpg|thumb|alt=Black and white photograph of a man with a short moustache and earrings, wearing a fur lined dress jacket, bow tie and fur hat|upright|[[Mixed-blood]] [[North American fur trade|fur trader]], {{circa|1870}}]]

The [[Métis]] are people descended from marriages between Europeans (mainly French)<ref>{{cite book |last=Rinella |first=Steven |title=American Buffalo: In Search of A Lost Icon |access-date=October 18, 2009 |year=2008 |publisher=Spiegel and Grau |location=NY |isbn=978-0-385-52168-0 |page=[https://archive.org/details/americanbuffaloi00rine/page/166 166] |url=https://archive.org/details/americanbuffaloi00rine|url-access=registration }}
</ref> and [[Cree]], [[Ojibwe]], [[Algonquin people|Algonquin]], [[Saulteaux]], [[Menominee]], [[Mi'kmaq]], [[Maliseet]], and other First Nations.<ref name=testt>{{cite web|title=What to Search: Topics-Canadian Genealogy Centre-Library and Archives Canada |work=Ethno-Cultural and Aboriginal Groups |publisher=Government of Canada |date=May 27, 2009 |url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/genealogie/022-905.004-e.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090705022732/http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/genealogie/022-905.004-e.html |archive-date=July 5, 2009 |access-date=October 2, 2009}}</ref> Their history dates to the mid-17th century.<ref name="First Nations Culture Areas Index"/>

When Europeans first arrived to Canada they relied on Indigenous peoples for fur trading skills and survival. To ensure alliances, relationships between European fur traders and Indigenous women were often consolidated through marriage.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Racism, Colonization and Indigeneity in Canada |last=Stevenson |first=Winona |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2011 |location=Ontario, Canada |pages=44–45}}</ref> The Métis homeland consists of the [[Provinces and territories of Canada|Canadian provinces]] of [[British Columbia]], [[Alberta]], [[Saskatchewan]], [[Manitoba]], and [[Ontario]], as well as the [[Northwest Territories]] (NWT).<ref>{{cite book |last=Howard |first=James H |title=The Plains-Ojibwa or Bungi: hunters and warriors of the Northern Prairies with special reference to the Turtle Mountain band |edition=Museum Anthropology Papers 1 |year=1965 |publisher=[[University of South Dakota]] |isbn=978-0-16-050400-6}}
</ref>

Amongst notable Métis people are singer and actor [[Tom Jackson (actor)|Tom Jackson]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/singer-tom-jackson-pitches-housing-complex-for-winnipeg-1.836550 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091025092455/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/singer-tom-jackson-pitches-housing-complex-for-winnipeg-1.836550 |archive-date=October 25, 2009 |title=Singer Tom Jackson pitches housing complex for Winnipeg |publisher=CBC |location=Canada |date=October 23, 2009 |access-date=January 27, 2011}}</ref> [[Commissioner of the Northwest Territories]] [[Tony Whitford]], and [[Louis Riel]] who led two resistance movements: the [[Red River Rebellion]] of 1869–1870 and the [[North-West Rebellion]] of 1885, which ended in his [[Trial of Louis Riel|trial]] and subsequent execution.<ref name="LouisRielCE">{{cite encyclopedia |first=George F.G. |last=Stanley |others=revised by Adam Gaudry |encyclopedia=[[The Canadian Encyclopedia]] |publisher=[[Historica Canada]] |title=Louis Riel |date=April 22, 2013 |url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/louis-riel}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |publisher=A database of materials held by the University of Saskatchewan Libraries and the University Archives |title=Louis Riel |url=http://library2.usask.ca/northwest/background/riel.htm |access-date=September 23, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070925032219/http://library2.usask.ca/northwest/background/riel.htm |archive-date=September 25, 2007 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Backgrounder Biography of Anthony W. J. (Tony) Whitford – NWT Commissioner|publisher=Indian and Northern Affairs Canada|work=2005 News Releases|date=October 28, 2008|url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ai/mr/nr/j-a2005/02623bk-eng.asp|access-date=October 6, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613194048/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ai/mr/nr/j-a2005/02623bk-eng.asp|archive-date=June 13, 2011}}</ref>

The languages inherently Métis are either [[Métis French]] or a mixed language called [[Michif]]. Michif, Mechif or Métchif is a [[Pronunciation respelling|phonetic spelling]] of Métif, a variant of Métis.<ref name=mist>{{cite book |url=http://metisresourcecentre.mb.ca/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=72&Itemid=13 |title=The Problem of Michif |publisher=Peter Bakker-Metis Resource Centre |isbn=978-0-19-509711-5 |access-date=October 5, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706184843/http://metisresourcecentre.mb.ca/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=72&Itemid=13 |archive-date=July 6, 2011  |year=1997 }}</ref> The Métis today predominantly speak [[Canadian English|English]], with [[Canadian French|French]] a strong second language, as well as numerous [[Indigenous languages of the Americas|Indigenous tongues]]. A 19th-century community of the Métis people, the [[Anglo-Métis]], were referred to as Countryborn. They were children of [[Rupert's Land]] fur trade typically of [[Orcadians|Orcadian]], Scottish, or English paternal descent and Indigenous maternal descent.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Barkwell |first1=Lawrence J. |first2=Leah |last2=Dorion |first3=Audreen |last3=Hourie |title=Metis legacy Michif culture, heritage, and folkways |volume=Metis legacy series, v. 2. |year=2006 |publisher=[[Gabriel Dumont Institute]] |location=Saskatoon, SK |isbn=978-0-920915-80-6}}
</ref> Their first languages would have been Indigenous ([[Cree language|Cree]], [[Western Ojibwa language|Saulteaux]], [[Assiniboine language|Assiniboine]], etc.) and English. Their fathers often spoke [[Canadian Gaelic|Gaelic]] or the [[Orcadian dialect]], thus leading to the development of an English dialect referred to as "[[Bungi dialect|Bungi]]".<ref>{{cite web |title=The Red River dialect |last=Blain |first=Eleanor M. |year=1994 |publisher=Winnipeg: Wuerz Publishing |url=http://tceplus.com/index.cfm?PgNm=TCE&Params=A1ARTA0001097 |access-date=October 15, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080315101109/http://tceplus.com/index.cfm?PgNm=TCE&Params=A1ARTA0001097 |archive-date=March 15, 2008  }}</ref>{{Dubious||date=July 2020|reason=Gaelic and English are different languages with different ancestry – English dialects are not descended from Gaelic.}}

S.35 of the ''Constitution Act, 1982'' mentions the Métis yet there has long been debate over legally defining the term Métis,<ref name="Foster2006gh">{{cite book |first=Martha |last=Harroun Foster |title=We know who we are: Métis identity in a Montana community |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JAI1vW_wyKAC&pg=PA12 |date=January 2006 |publisher=University of Oklahoma Press |isbn=978-0-8061-3705-6 |page=12}}</ref> but on September 23, 2003, the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] ruled that Métis are a distinct people with significant rights ([[R v Powley|Powley ruling]]).<ref name=pow>{{cite web |url=http://www.canlii.org/en/ca/scc/doc/2003/2003scc43/2003scc43.pdf |title=Her Majesty The Queen vs. Steve Powley and Roddy Charles Powley (R. v. Powley, 2 S.C.R. 207, 2003 SCC 43) |publisher=Federation of Law Societies of Canada |year=2003 |access-date=March 11, 2010}}</ref>

Unlike First Nations people, there has been no distinction between status and non-status Métis;<ref name="Company2005">{{cite book |author=Houghton Mifflin Company |title=The American Heritage guide to contemporary usage and style |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xb6ie6PqYhwC&pg=PA185 |date=September 28, 2005 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |isbn=978-0-618-60499-9 |page=185}}</ref> the Métis, their heritage and Indigenous ancestry have often been absorbed and assimilated into their surrounding populations.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Barkwell |first1=Lawrence J. |first2=Leah |last2=Dorion |first3=Darren |last3=Prefontaine |title=Metis Legacy: A Historiography and Annotated Bibliography |year=2001 |publisher=Pemmican Publications Inc. and Saskatoon: Gabriel Dumont Institute |location=Winnipeg, MB |isbn=978-1-894717-03-8}}
</ref>

===Forced assimilation===
{{Main|Canadian genocide of Indigenous peoples|Settler colonialism in Canada}}

From the late 18th century, European Canadians (and the Canadian government) encouraged [[Cultural assimilation|assimilation]] of Indigenous culture into what was referred to as "[[Culture of Canada|Canadian culture]]."<ref name="RoyalCom-sg3">{{cite web |publisher=Indian and Northern Affairs Canada |title=Stage Three: Displacement and Assimilation |date=February 8, 2006 |url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ch/rcap/sg/sgm6_e.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030621180528/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ch/rcap/sg/sgm6_e.html |archive-date=June 21, 2003 |access-date=October 3, 2009 |via=Government of Canada Web Archive}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Report of the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples |chapter=Stage Three: Displacement and Assimilation |date=February 8, 2006 |url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ch/rcap/sg/sgmm_e.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030608024259/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ch/rcap/sg/sgmm_e.html |archive-date=June 8, 2003 |access-date=October 3, 2009}}</ref> These attempts reached a climax in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with a series of initiatives that aimed at complete assimilation and subjugation of the Indigenous peoples. These policies, which were made possible by legislation such as the ''[[Gradual Civilization Act]]''<ref name=gradcivact>{{cite web |title=Gradual Civilization Act, 1857 |url=http://caid.ca/GraCivAct1857.pdf |publisher=Government of Canada |access-date=October 17, 2015}}</ref> and the ''Indian Act'',<ref name="Indian Act"/> focused on European ideals of Christianity, sedentary living, agriculture, and education.<ref name="h269">{{cite web | title=What the debate around Indigenous genocide says about Canada | website=Macleans.ca | date=Jun 7, 2019 | url=https://macleans.ca/news/canada/what-the-debate-around-indigenous-genocide-says-about-canada/ | access-date=Nov 20, 2024}}</ref>

====Christianization====
[[File:Study period at Roman Catholic Indian Residential School, Fort Resolution, NWT (14112957392).jpg|thumb|right|Study period at a [[Roman Catholic]] Indian Residential School in [[Fort Resolution]], [[Northwest Territories|NWT]]| alt=Indigenous children working at long desks]]

[[Missionary|Missionary work]] directed at the Indigenous people of Canada had been ongoing since the first missionaries arrived in the 1600s, generally from France, some of whom were martyred ([[List of saints of the Society of Jesus|Jesuit saints]] called the [[Canadian Martyrs]]). [[Christianization]] as government policy became more systematic with the ''Indian Act'' in 1876, which would bring new sanctions for those who did not [[Conversion to Christianity|convert to Christianity]]. For example, the new laws would prevent non-Christian Indigenous people from testifying or having their cases heard in court, and ban alcohol consumption.<ref name="Armitage">{{cite book |last1=Armitage |first1=Andrew |title=Comparing the Policy of Aboriginal Assimilation: Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. |date=1995 |publisher=University of British Columbia Press |location=Vancouver, Canada |pages=77–78 }}</ref> When the ''Indian Act'' was amended in 1884, traditional religious and social practices, such as the [[Potlatch]], would be banned, and further amendments in 1920 would prevent "[[Indian Register|status Indians]]" (as defined in the ''Act'') from wearing traditional dress or performing traditional dances in an attempt to stop all non-Christian practices.<ref name="Armitage" />

====Sedentary living, reserves, and "gradual civilization"====
Another focus of the Canadian government was to make the Indigenous groups of Canada sedentary, as they thought that this would make them easier to assimilate. In the 19th century, the government began to support the creation of model farming villages, which were meant to encourage non-sedentary Indigenous groups to settle in an area and begin to cultivate agriculture.<ref name="Doesett">{{cite journal |last1=Dorsett |first1=Shaunnagh |title=Civilisation and Cultivation: Colonial Policy and Indigenous Peoples in Canada and Australia |journal=Griffith Law Review |date=1995 |volume=4 |issue=2 |page=219}}</ref> When most of these model farming villages failed,<ref name="Doesett" /> the government turned instead to the creation of [[Indian reserve]]s with the ''[[Indian Act]]'' of 1876.<ref name="Indian Act">{{cite web|title=Indian Act |url=http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/i-5/ |publisher=Government of Canada |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216033916/http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/I-5/ |archive-date=February 16, 2013  |date=April 8, 2019 }}</ref> With the creation of these reserves came many restricting laws, such as further bans on all intoxicants, restrictions on eligibility to vote in band elections, decreased hunting and fishing areas, and inability for status Indians to visit other groups on their reserves.<ref name="Indian Act" /> Farming was still seen as an important practice for assimilation on reserves; however, by the late 19th century the government had instituted restrictive policies here too, such as the [[Peasant Farm Policy]], which restricted reserve farmers largely to the use of hand tools.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Buckley |first=Helen |title=From Wooden Ploughs to Welfare: Why Indian policy failed in the Prairie provinces |publisher=McGill-Queen's University Press |year=1992 |isbn=0-7735-0893-7 |location=Montreal and Kingston |pages=52–53 |language=en}}</ref> This was implemented largely to limit the competitiveness of First Nations farming.<ref>{{Cite book |last=[[Sarah Carter (historian)|Carter, Sarah]] |title=Lost Harvests: Prairie Indian reserve farmers and government policy |publisher=McGill-Queen's University Press |year=1990 |isbn=0-7735-0755-8 |location=Montreal and Kingston |page=193 |language=en}}</ref>

Through the ''[[Gradual Civilization Act]]'' in 1857, the government would encourage Indians (i.e., First Nations) to ''[[Suffrage|enfranchise]]'' – to ''remove all legal distinctions between [Indians] and Her Majesty's other Canadian Subjects''.<ref name="gradcivact" /> If an Indigenous chose to enfranchise, it would strip them and their family of [[Aboriginal title]], with the idea that they would become "less savage" and "more civilized," thus become assimilated into Canadian society.<ref name="Miller">{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=J. R. |title=Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens: A History of Indian-White Relations in Canada |date=2000 |publisher=University of Toronto Press |location=Toronto, Canada |page=140 }}</ref> However, they were often still defined as ''non-citizens'' by Europeans, and those few who did enfranchise were often met with disappointment.<ref name="Miller" />

====Residential system====
{{main|Canadian Indian residential school system|Residential school denialism}}
[[File:Stpauls-middlechurch-man.jpg|thumb|left|St. Paul's Indian Industrial School, Middlechurch, Manitoba, 1901]]
The final government strategy of assimilation, made possible by the ''Indian Act'' was the [[Canadian Indian residential school system|Canadian residential school system]]:

{{Blockquote|Of all the initiatives that were undertaken in the first century of Confederation, none was more ambitious or central to the civilizing strategy of the Department, to its goal of assimilation than the residential school system… it was the residential school experience that would lead children most effectively out of their "savage" communities into "higher civilization" and "full citizenship."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Milloy |first1=John |title=A National Crime: The Canadian Government and the Residential School System, 1879 to 1986 |date=1999 |publisher=University of Manitoba Press |location=Winnipeg, Canada |pages=21–22 }}</ref>}}

Beginning in 1874 and lasting until 1996, the Canadian government, in partnership with the dominant Christian Churches, ran 130 residential boarding schools across Canada for Indigenous children. Sometimes school attendance was forced.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Popic |first1=Linda |title=Compensating Canada's 'Stolen Generations' |journal=Journal of Aboriginal History |date=2008 |page=14 |issue=December 2007 – January 2008}}</ref> While the schools provided some education, they were plagued by under-funding, disease, and abuse.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Charles |first1=Grant |last2=DeGane |first2=Mike |title=Student-to-Student Abuse in the Indian Residential Schools in Canada: Setting the Stage for Further Understanding |journal=Child & Youth Services |date=2013 |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=343–359 |doi=10.1080/0145935X.2013.859903 |s2cid=144148882 }}</ref>

According to some scholars, the Canadian government's laws and policies, including the residential school system, that encouraged or required Indigenous peoples to [[Cultural imperialism|assimilate]] into a [[Eurocentrism|Eurocentric]] society, violated the [[United Nations]] [[Genocide Convention]] that Canada signed in 1949 and passed through Parliament in 1952. Therefore, these scholars believe that Canada could be tried in [[international court]] for [[genocide]].<ref name="Restoule, Jean-Paul 2002">{{cite book |last=Restoule |first=Jean-Paul |title=Aboriginal Identity: The Need for Historical and Contextual Perspectives |volume=24 |issue=2 |access-date=October 28, 2009 |year=2002 |publisher=Pearson/Prentice Hall |location=Toronto, ON |pages=102–12 |chapter-url=http://eric.ed.gov/ERICWebPortal/detail?accno=EJ630059 |chapter=Seeing Ourselves. John Macionis and Nijole v. Benokraitis and Bruce Ravelli}}</ref> A legal case resulted in settlement of {{CAD|2 billion}} in 2006 and the 2008 establishment of the [[Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada|Truth and Reconciliation Commission]], which confirmed the injurious effect on children of this system and turmoil created between Indigenous peoples and non-Indigenous peoples.<ref name="T&RC">{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-17161893 |title=Canada commission issues details abuse of native children |author=Unattributed |date=February 25, 2012 |publisher=BBC |access-date=February 25, 2012}}</ref> In 2008, Prime Minister [[Stephen Harper]] issued an apology on behalf of the Canadian government and its citizens for the residential school system.<ref>{{cite news |last=Benjoe |first=Kerry |title=Group gathers for Harper's apology |newspaper=The Leader-Post |date=June 12, 2008 |url=http://www2.canada.com/reginaleaderpost/news/story.html?id=2e362bf9-0f5a-43c6-ab5e-81a276b4767c |access-date=October 2, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120915023426/http://www2.canada.com/reginaleaderpost/news/story.html?id=2e362bf9-0f5a-43c6-ab5e-81a276b4767c |archive-date=September 15, 2012  }}
</ref>

==Politics, law, and legislation==
{{See also|Monarchy of Canada and the Indigenous peoples of Canada}}

===Indigenous law vs. Aboriginal law===
{{further|Canadian Indigenous law}}
The term ''[[Canadian Indigenous law]]'' refers to Indigenous peoples' own legal systems. This includes the laws and legal processes developed by Indigenous groups to govern their relationships, manage their natural resources, and manage conflicts.<ref name=Borrows>{{cite web 
|url= http://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2008/lcc-cdc/JL2-66-2006E.pdf
|title= Indigenous Legal Traditions in Canada |author= John Borrows 
|date= 2006|work= Report for the Law Commission of Canada |publisher= Law Foundation Chair in Aboriginal Justice and Governance Faculty of Law, University of Victoria|quote= In Canada, Indigenous legal traditions are separate from but interact with common law and civil law to produce a variety of rights and obligations for Indigenous people....Many Indigenous societies in Canada possess legal traditions. These traditions have indeterminate status in the eyes of many Canadian institutions. }}</ref> [[Indigenous law]] is developed from a variety of sources and institutions, which differ across legal traditions.<ref name=Guides>{{Cite web|url=https://guides.library.queensu.ca/Aboriginal-and-Indigenous-law/introductory|title=Research Guides: Aboriginal Law & Indigenous Laws: A note on terms|first=Amy|last=Kaufman|website=guides.library.queensu.ca|quote="Indigenous law exists as a source of law apart from the common and civil legal traditions in Canada. Importantly, Indigenous laws also exist apart from Aboriginal law, though these sources of law are interconnected. Aboriginal law is a body of law, made by the courts and legislatures, that largely deals with the unique constitutional rights of Aboriginal peoples and the relationship between Aboriginal peoples and the Crown. Aboriginal law is largely found in colonial instruments (such as the Royal Proclamation of 1763, the Constitution Acts of 1867 and 1982 and the Indian Act) and court decisions, but also includes sources of Indigenous law. "Indigenous law consists of legal orders which are rooted in Indigenous societies themselves. It arises from communities and First Nation groups across the country, such as Nuu Chah Nulth, Haida, Coast Salish, Tsimshian, Heiltsuk, and may include relationships to the land, the spirit world, creation stories, customs, processes of deliberation and persuasion, codes of conduct, rules, teachings and axioms for living and governing."}}</ref> [[Canadian Aboriginal law]]  is the area of law related to the Canadian government's relationship with the Indigenous peoples. Section 91(24) of the ''Constitution Act, 1867'' gives the federal parliament exclusive power to legislate in matters related to Aboriginals, which includes groups governed by the ''Indian Act'', different Numbered Treaties and outside of those acts.<ref name="LeuprechtRussell2011">{{cite book|author1=Christian Leuprecht|author2=Peter H. Russell |title=Essential Readings in Canadian Constitutional Politics |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kDN1WzoaFNEC&pg=PA477 |year=2011 |publisher=University of Toronto Press|isbn=978-1-4426-0368-4|page=477}}</ref>

===Treaties===
[[File:Medal-Viki.jpg|thumb|alt=Photograph showing the two sides of a round silver medal, showing the profile of Queen Victoria on one side and the inscription "Victoria Regina", with the other side having a depiction of a man in European garb shaking hands with a man in historical First Nation clothing with the inscription "Indian Treaty 187"|The Indian Chiefs Medal, presented to commemorate [[Numbered Treaties|Treaties]] [[Treaty 3|3]], [[Treaty 4|4]], [[Treaty 5|5]], [[Treaty 6|6]] and [[Treaty 7|7]], bearing the image of [[Queen Victoria]]]]

The [[Monarchy of Canada and the Indigenous peoples of Canada]] began [[Timeline of the European colonization of North America|interactions in North America]] during the European colonization period. The Royal Proclamation of 1763 recognized Indigenous title and the [[Treaty of Niagara]] of 1764 bound the Crown and the Indigenous peoples of the Great Lakes basin together in a familial relationship, a relationship that exists to this day, exemplified by First Nations attendance at the coronation of [[King Charles III]].{{sfn |Cote |Tidridge |2024 |p=43}} Post-Confederation Canada adopted a paternalistic approach and imposed an approach as though the nation-to-nation relationship did not exist, administering relations solely under Canadian law.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}}

After Canada's acquisition of [[Rupert's Land]] and the [[North-Western Territory]] in 1870, the eleven [[Numbered Treaties]] were imposed on the First Nations from 1871 to 1921. These treaties are agreements with the Crown administered by [[Canadian Aboriginal law]] and overseen by the [[Minister of Crown–Indigenous Relations]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Hall|first=Anthony J.|date=June 6, 2011|title=Treaties with Indigenous Peoples in Canada {{!}} The Canadian Encyclopedia|url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/aboriginal-treaties |access-date=August 5, 2021|website=www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca}}</ref>

Treaty rights would be recognized and incorporated into the 1982 Constitution. Many agreements signed before the [[Canadian Confederation|Confederation of Canada]] are recognized in Canadian law, such as the [[Peace and Friendship Treaties]], the [[Robinson Treaties]], the [[Douglas Treaties]], and many others, although many First Nations still have no treaty with the Crown recognizing their title, such as the Mikmaq, the Anishnaabe and several northern British Columbia nations.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}}

For many years, Canada did not negotiate with First Nations to address [[Indigenous land claims in Canada|their aboriginal title]]. Canadian court judgments and political pressure led to a change in ways following the [[Canadian Centennial]] year. The first treaty implemented under the new framework was the ''[[James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement]]'' in 1970 between the Cree and Quebec. This was followed by the ''Inuvialuit Final Agreement'' in 1984 that led to the creation of the [[Inuvialuit Settlement Region]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://irc.inuvialuit.com/about-irc/inuvialuit-final-agreement/ |title=Inuvialuit Final Agreement |access-date=August 19, 2024 |publisher=Inuvialuit Regional Corporation}}</ref> The [[Nunavut Land Claims Agreement]] of 1993 lead to the creation of the [[Inuit]]-majority territory of [[Nunavut]] later that decade. The Canadian Crown continues to sign new treaties with Indigenous peoples, notably though the [[British Columbia Treaty Process]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Crowe|first=Keith|date=March 2, 2015|title=Comprehensive Land Claims: Modern Treaties {{!}} The Canadian Encyclopedia |url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/comprehensive-land-claims-modern-treaties |access-date=August 5, 2021|website=www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca}}</ref>

According to the ''First Nations–Federal Crown Political Accord'', "cooperation will be a cornerstone for partnership between Canada and First Nations, wherein ''Canada'' is the short-form reference to [[Style of the British sovereign|Her Majesty the Queen]] in Right of Canada.<ref name="FN" /> The Supreme Court of Canada argued that treaties "served to reconcile pre-existing Indigenous sovereignty with assumed Crown sovereignty, and to define Aboriginal rights."<ref name="FN" /> First Nations interpreted agreements covered in [[Treaty 8]] to last "as long as the sun shines, grass grows and rivers flow."<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/background/aboriginals/treaty8.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040807043635/http://www.cbc.ca/news/background/aboriginals/treaty8.html |archive-date=August 7, 2004 |title=What is Treaty 8? |via=cbc.ca |publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |access-date=October 5, 2009}}</ref> However, the Canadian government has frequently breached the Crown's treaty obligations over the years, and tries to address these issues by negotiating [[Indigenous specific land claims in Canada|specific land claim]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Albers|first=Gretchen|date=March 2, 2015|title=Indigenous Peoples and Specific Claims {{!}} The Canadian Encyclopedia|url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/specific-claims |access-date=August 5, 2021|website=www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca}}</ref>

===''Indian Act''===
{{Main|Indian Act}}

[[File:Crombie1983.jpg|thumb|alt=Colour photograph of former federal Indian affairs minister David Crombie speaking to reporters on the floor of the 1983 Progressive Conservative leadership convention|Former federal Indian affairs minister [[David Crombie]] was responsible for Bill C-31.]]

The ''Indian Act'' is Canadian law that dates from 1876. The Act replaced pre-Confederation Canadian laws, and was intended to administer the Indigenous people, and define Canadian interactions. Successive Canadian governments used its powers to impose conditions on the First Nations, and guide their integration into Canada. Today still, the ''Indian Act'' indicates how reserves and bands can operate and defines who is recognized as an "Indian."<ref name="laws">{{cite web| title = The Indian Act| work = Indian Act. Current to March 16, 2014| publisher = Department of Justice Canada| date = March 16, 2014| url = http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/PDF/I-5.pdf}}</ref> There have been many updates to this law since then, allowing Canadian citizenship and voting rights among others.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Education |first=Elections Canada's Civic |title=First Nations Peoples and the Right to Vote Case Study |url=https://electionsanddemocracy.ca/voting-rights-through-time-0/first-nations-and-right-vote-case-study |access-date=2026-09-22 |website=electionsanddemocracy.ca |language=en}}</ref>

In 1985, the Canadian Parliament passed Bill C-31, ''An Act to Amend the Indian Act''. Because of a constitutional requirement, the bill took effect on April 17, 1985.<ref name="bill">{{cite web|title = First Nations, Bill C-31, Indian Act|work = Communications Branch|publisher = Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development|url = http://www.johnco.com/nativel/bill_c31.html|access-date = October 2, 2009|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090730192508/http://www.johnco.com/nativel/bill_c31.html|archive-date = July 30, 2009|df = mdy-all}}</ref>
* It ends discriminatory provisions of the ''Indian Act'', especially those that discriminated against women.<ref name="bill"/>
* It changes the meaning of ''status'' and for the first time allows for limited reinstatement of Indians who were denied or lost status or band membership.<ref name="bill"/>
* It allows bands to define their own membership rules.<ref name="bill"/>

Those people accepted into band membership under band rules may not be status Indians. C-31 clarified that various sections of the ''Indian Act'' apply to band members. The sections under debate concern community life and land holdings. Sections pertaining to Indians (First Nations peoples) as individuals (in this case, wills and taxation of personal property) were not included.<ref name="bill"/>

===Royal Commission===
{{Main|Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples}}

[[File:TRC in the Community (Map 1) without captions.svg|thumb|Map with areas labelled where the [[Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada]] took part in outreach and statement gathering events over the impact of [[Canadian residential schools]] with the Indigenous peoples of Canada]]

The [[Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples]] was a [[royal commission]] undertaken by the Government of Canada in 1991 to address issues of the Indigenous peoples of Canada.<ref name=royal/> It assessed past government policies toward Indigenous people, such as residential schools, and provided policy recommendations to the government.<ref name="Cairns200j0">{{cite book|first=Alan |last=Cairns |title=Citizens plus: aboriginal peoples and the Canadian state|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TmQ_T6XSPFIC&pg=PA116|year=2000|publisher=UBC Press|isbn=978-0-7748-0767-8|page=116}}</ref> The Commission issued its final report in November 1996. The five-volume, 4,000-page report covered a vast range of issues; its 440 recommendations called for sweeping changes to the interaction between Indigenous, non-Indigenous people and the governments in Canada.<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=http://www.iog.ca/publications/healthrcap.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030614014908/http://iog.ca/publications/healthrcap.pdf |archive-date=June 14, 2003 |title=Summary of the Final Report of The Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples: Implications for Canada's Health Care System |publisher=The Institute on Governance |access-date=October 5, 2009}}</ref> The report "set out a 20-year agenda for change."<ref name="McCaslinCentre2005fu">{{cite book|first1=Wanda D. |last1=McCaslin |author2=University of Saskatchewan. Native Law Centre |title=Justice as healing: indigenous ways |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HOCsEIqU-pEC&pg=PA27|date=July 2005|publisher=Living Justice Press|isbn=978-0-9721886-1-6|page=27}}</ref>

===Health policy===
{{Main|Indian Health Transfer Policy}}

In 1995, the Government of Canada announced the Aboriginal Right to Self-Government Policy.<ref>{{cite web|title = Aboriginal Health & Cultural Diversity Glossary|publisher = [[University of Saskatchewan]], College of Nursing|year = 2003|url = https://www.usask.ca/nursing/aboriginalglossary/i.htm|access-date = October 2, 2009|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091024031441/http://www.usask.ca/nursing/aboriginalglossary/i.htm|archive-date = October 24, 2009|df = mdy-all}}</ref> This policy recognizes that First Nations and Inuit have the constitutional right to shape their own forms of government to suit their particular historical, cultural, political and economic circumstances. The [[Indian Health Transfer Policy]] provided a framework for the assumption of control of health services by Indigenous peoples, and set forth a developmental approach to transfer centred on self-determination in health.<ref>{{cite book| last1 =Jacklin |first1 =Kristen |first2= Wayne |last2=Warry| editor1-first=Arachu |editor1-last=Castro |editor2-first=Merrill |editor2-last=Singer| title = Unhealthy health policy: a critical anthropological examination|chapter=14 Then Indian Health Transfer Policy in Canada: Toward Self-Determination or Cost Containment?| publisher = Rowman Altamira|place=Oxford United Kingdom| year = 2004| page = 215| chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=XWbF_tfYUuEC&pg=PA215| isbn =978-0-7591-0510-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title = Indian Health Policy 1979 |via=hc-sc.gc.ca | publisher = Health Canada| date = October 25, 2007| url = http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/ahc-asc/branch-dirgen/fnihb-dgspni/poli_1979-eng.php| author= First Nations & Inuit Health Branch| access-date =October 2, 2009 }}</ref> Through this process, the decision to enter transfer discussions with [[Health Canada]] rests with each community. Once involved in transfer, communities can take control of health programme responsibilities at a pace determined by their individual circumstances and health management capabilities.<ref>{{cite web|last=Lemchuk-Favel|first=Laurel|title=Financing a First Nations and Inuit Integrated Health System A Discussion Document|publisher=Health Canada |via=hc-sc.gc.ca|date=February 22, 1999|url=http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/fniah-spnia/alt_formats/fnihb-dgspni/pdf/pubs/agree-accord/1999_finance_integr-eng.pdf|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20130111060520/http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/fniah-spnia/alt_formats/fnihb-dgspni/pdf/pubs/agree-accord/1999_finance_integr-eng.pdf|archive-date=January 11, 2013|access-date=October 2, 2009}}</ref> The [[National Aboriginal Health Organization]] (NAHO) incorporated in 2000, was an Indigenous -designed and-controlled not-for-profit body in Canada that worked to influence and advance the health and well-being of Indigenous Peoples.<ref name="WaldramHerring2006">{{cite book|first1=James Burgess |last1=Waldram  |author-link=James B. Waldram |first2=Ann |last2=Herring |first3=T. Kue |last3=Young |title=Aboriginal health in Canada: historical, cultural, and epidemiological perspectives |date=July 30, 2006|publisher=University of Toronto Press|isbn=978-0-8020-8579-5|page=85}}</ref> Its funding was discontinued in 2012.<ref>{{Cite news |date=April 9, 2012 |title=National Aboriginal Health Organization’s funding cut |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/national-aboriginal-health-organization-s-funding-cut-1.1194520 |access-date=September 22, 2026 |work=[[CBC News]]}}</ref>

===Political organization===
{{Further|Band government|History of Indigenous organizations in Canada}}

First Nations and Inuit organizations ranged in size from [[Band society|band societies]] of a few people to multi-nation confederacies like the Iroquois. First Nations leaders from across the country formed the [[Assembly of First Nations]], which began as the National Indian Brotherhood in 1968.<ref name="price">{{cite book |last=Price |first=Richard |title=The Spirit of the Alberta Indian Treaties |publisher=University of Alberta Press > the University of Michigan |year=1999 |isbn=978-0-88864-327-8 |url=https://archive.org/details/spiritofalbertai0s65unse }}</ref> Métis and Inuit are represented nationally by the [[Métis National Council]] and [[Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami]] respectively.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}}

Today's political organizations have resulted from interaction with European-style methods of government through the [[Federal Interlocutor for Métis and Non-Status Indians]]. Indigenous political organizations throughout Canada vary in political standing, viewpoints, and reasons for forming.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/aboriginal-heritage/020016-4010-e.html|title=Post-war Rise of Political Organizations|work=Library and Archives Canada| access-date =October 6, 2009}}</ref> First Nations, Métis and Inuit negotiate with the Government of Canada through [[Crown–Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada]] in all affairs concerning land, entitlement, and rights.<ref name="price"/> The First Nation groups that operate independently do not belong to these groups.<ref name="price"/>

==Culture==
{{See also|Mythologies of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas}}
[[File:Snow Shoe Maker between ca. 1900-1930.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=Black and white photo of a woman kneeling on the ground making a snowshoe. She is wearing a plaid shirt and white dress locking down at the snowshoe. Around her is four frames of snowshoe to be made leaning on a tippy, |Traditional [[snowshoe]] maker, {{circa|1900}}]]

Countless Indigenous words, inventions and games have become an everyday part of [[Languages of Canada|Canadian language]] and use. The [[canoe]], [[snowshoe]]s, the [[toboggan]], [[lacrosse]], [[tug of war]], [[maple syrup]] and tobacco are just a few of the products, inventions and games.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.edu.gov.mb.ca/k12/cur/socstud/foundation_gr2/blms/2-2-1c.pdf |title=Diverse Peoples – Aboriginal Contributions and Inventions|work=The Government of Manitoba| access-date =October 17, 2009 }}</ref> Some of the words include the [[barbecue]], [[Reindeer|caribou]], [[chipmunk]], [[Groundhog|woodchuck]], [[hammock]], [[skunk]], and [[moose]].<ref name=Edinburgh>{{cite web|last=Newhouse |first=David |url=http://www.cst.ed.ac.uk/2005conference/papers/Newhouse_paper.pdf |title=Hidden in Plain Sight Aboriginal Contributions to Canada and Canadian Identity Creating a new Indian Problem |work=Centre of Canadian Studies, University of Edinburgh |access-date=October 17, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723221908/http://www.cst.ed.ac.uk/2005conference/papers/Newhouse_paper.pdf |archive-date=July 23, 2011  }}</ref>

[[List of place names in Canada of Indigenous origin|Many places in Canada]], both natural features and human habitations, use Indigenous names. The word ''Canada'' itself derives from the [[Laurentian language|St. Lawrence Iroquoian]] word meaning 'village' or 'settlement'.<ref>{{cite book|first1=Bruce G. |last1=Trigger |first2=James F. |last2=Pendergast |year=1978 |chapter=Saint-Lawrence Iroquoians |title=Handbook of North American Indians |volume=15 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |pages= 357–361|isbn=978-0-16-004575-2}}</ref> The province of Saskatchewan derives its name from the [[Saskatchewan River]], which in the Cree language is called ''Kisiskatchewani Sipi'', meaning 'swift-flowing river'.<ref name="places" /> ''[[Ottawa]]'', the name of Canada's capital city, comes from the [[Algonquin language]] term ''adawe'', meaning 'to trade'.<ref name="places">{{cite web|url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ai/mr/is/info106-eng.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090126183335/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ai/mr/is/info106-eng.asp |archive-date=January 26, 2009 |title=Aboriginal place names contribute to a rich tapestry |work=Indian and Northern Affairs Canada |access-date=October 17, 2009}}</ref>

Modern youth groups, such as [[Scouts Canada]] and the [[Girl Guides of Canada]], include programs based largely on Indigenous lore, arts and crafts, character building and outdoor camp craft and living.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.scouting.org/scoutsource/CubScouts/AboutCubScouts/history.aspx |title=History of Cub Scouting |work=Boy Scouts of America |access-date=October 17, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091031045900/http://www.scouting.org/scoutsource/CubScouts/AboutCubScouts/history.aspx |archive-date=October 31, 2009  }}</ref>

Indigenous cultural areas depend upon their ancestors' primary [[Society#Types|lifeway]], or occupation, at the time of European contact. These culture areas correspond closely with [[geography of Canada|physical and ecological]] [[List of regions in Canada|regions of Canada]].<ref name="three1">{{cite book|editor=Goddard, Ives|others=W. C. Sturtevant|title=Languages. Handbook of North American Indians|volume=17|year=1996|publisher=Smithsonian Institution|location=[[Washington, D.C.|Washington, D. C.]]|isbn=978-0-16-048774-3}}</ref> The [[Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast]] were centred around ocean and river fishing; in the interior of British Columbia, hunter-gatherer and river fishing. In both of these areas, the salmon was of chief importance. For the people of the plains, bison hunting was the primary activity. In the [[taiga|subarctic forest]], other species such as the moose were more important. For peoples near the [[Great Lakes]] and [[St. Lawrence River]], [[Shifting cultivation|shifting agriculture]] was practised, including the raising of [[maize]], [[bean]]s, and [[Cucurbita|squash]].<ref name="three2" /><ref name="three1" /> While for Inuit, hunting was the primary source of food with [[Pinniped|seals]] the primary component of their diet.<ref name="Searles">{{cite journal|last=Searles|first=Edmund|journal=Food & Foodways|pages=55–78|title=Food and the Making of Modern Inuit Identities |volume=10 |issue=1 |date=January 2002|doi=10.1080/07409710212485|s2cid=144692404|quote=Although the Inuit of the Canadian Arctic have access to an ever-expanding market of different kinds of foods, they continue to invest considerable time and money obtaining Inuit foods, that is, foods hunted, fished, and gathered within the Inuit homeland.}}</ref> The caribou, fish, other [[marine mammal]]s and to a lesser extent plants, berries and seaweed are part of the [[Inuit cuisine|Inuit diet]]. One of the most noticeable symbols of [[Inuit culture]], the [[inuksuk]] is the emblem of the [[Vancouver]] [[2010 Winter Olympics]]. ''Inuksuit'' are rock sculptures made by stacking stones; in the shape of a human figure, they are called ''inunnguaq''.<ref name=vancouver>{{cite web|url=http://www.vancouver2010.com/ |title=Vancouver 2010 Olympic Games Emblem |work=2010 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games |access-date=October 17, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091025194336/http://www.vancouver2010.com/ |archive-date=October 25, 2009  }}</ref>
[[File:Tsuu Tsina parade.JPG|thumb|left|alt=Colour photograph of Tsuu T'ina children in traditional costume on horseback at a Stampede Parade in front of an audience|[[Tsuutʼina Nation|Tsuu T'ina]] children at a parade]]

[[Indian reserve]]s, established in [[Law of Canada|Canadian law]] by treaties such as [[Treaty 7]], are lands of First Nations recognized by non-Indigenous governments.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uarctic.org/module_12_tmDGm.pdf.file+Land+Claims,+Ownership,+and+Co-management&hl=en&gl=ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050223032854/https://www.uarctic.org/bcs/BCS331/module_12.pdf |archive-date=February 23, 2005 |title=Land Claims, Ownership, and Co-management |work=Developed by Ken Coates, Dean, College of Arts and Sciences, University of Saskatchewan and Greg Poelzer, Chair, Political Science Program, [[University of Northern British Columbia]] |format=PDF |access-date=October 5, 2009}}</ref> Some reserves are within cities, such as the Opawikoscikan Reserve in [[Prince Albert, Saskatchewan]], [[Wendake]] in [[Quebec City]] or [[Enoch Cree Nation 135]] in the [[Edmonton Metropolitan Region]]. There are more reserves in Canada than there are First Nations, which were ceded multiple reserves by treaty.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.literacycommunity.com/grade3/firstnations/reserve.htm|title=The First Nations-Communities: Reserves|work=The Literacy Community|access-date=October 5, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091212191839/http://www.literacycommunity.com/grade3/firstnations/reserve.htm |archive-date=December 12, 2009 }}</ref> Indigenous people currently work in a variety of occupations and may live outside their ancestral homes. The traditional cultures of their ancestors, shaped by nature, still exert a strong influence on them, from spirituality to political attitudes.<ref name="three2" /><ref name="three1" /> [[National Indigenous Peoples Day]] is a day of recognition of the cultures and contributions of the First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples of Canada. The day was first celebrated in 1996, after it was proclaimed that year, by then [[Governor General of Canada]], [[Roméo LeBlanc]], to be celebrated on June 21 annually.<ref name=history>{{cite web |url=http://dsp-psd.pwgsc.gc.ca/Collection/R32-179-2000E.pdf|title=National Aboriginal Day History|work=Indian and Northern Affairs Canada | access-date =October 18, 2009}}</ref> Most provincial jurisdictions do not recognize it as a [[Public holidays in Canada|statutory holiday]].<ref name=history/>

===Languages===
{{Further|Indigenous languages of the Americas|Languages of Canada#Indigenousl languages}}
{{See also|Canadian Aboriginal syllabics}}

There are thirteen [[Languages of Canada#Indigenous languages|Indigenous language groups]], eleven oral and two [[sign language|sign]], in Canada, made up of more than sixty-five distinct dialects.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/2006/dp-pd/tbt/Rp-eng.cfm?LANG=E&APATH=3&DETAIL=0&DIM=0&FL=A&FREE=0&GC=0&GID=0&GK=0&GRP=1&PID=89149&PRID=0&PTYPE=88971,97154&S=0&SHOWALL=0&SUB=733&Temporal=2006&THEME=73&VID=0&VNAMEE=&VNAMEF=|title=Aboriginal languages|work=Statistics Canada|access-date =October 5, 2009}}</ref> Of these, only [[Cree language|Cree]], [[Inuktitut]], and [[Ojibwe language|Ojibwe]] have a large enough population of fluent speakers to be considered viable to survive in the long term.<ref name="online">{{cite book|last=Gordon|first=Raymond G. Jr.|title=Ethnologue: Languages of the world|place=Dallas, Texas|publisher=SIL International|year=2005|edition=15|format=Web Version online by SIL International, formerly known as the Summer Institute of Linguistics|url=http://www.ethnologue.com/web.asp|isbn=978-1-55671-159-6|access-date=October 6, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091012192013/http://www.ethnologue.com/web.asp|archive-date=October 12, 2009}}</ref> Two of Canada's territories give official status to native languages. In Nunavut, [[Inuktut]], also known as the [[Inuit languages|Inuit language]], (Inuktitut and [[Inuinnaqtun]]) are official languages alongside the national languages of English and French.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.itk.ca/projects/inuktut/ |title=Inuktut|access-date=June 17, 2024|publisher=[[Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami]]|website=www.itk.ca}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://langcom.nu.ca/en |title=Information|website=www.langcom.nu.ca|publisher=Office of the Languages Commissioner of Nunavut}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://langcom.nu.ca/investigation-process/your-linguistic-rights |title=Your Linguistic Rights|access-date=June 17, 2024|website=www.langcom.nu.ca|publisher=Office of the Languages Commissioner of Nunavut}}</ref>

In the Northwest Territories, the ''[[Northwest Territories#Languages|Official Languages Act]]'' declares that there are 11 different languages: [[Chipewyan language|Chipewyan]], Cree, English, French, [[Gwichʼin language|Gwichʼin]], Inuinnaqtun, Inuktitut, [[Inuvialuktun]], North [[Slavey language|Slavey]], South Slavey, and [[Dogrib language|Tłįchǫ]].<ref>{{cite web| title = Official Languages Act| work = Legislation Division, Department of Justice| year = 1988| url = http://www.justice.gov.nt.ca/PDF/ACTS/Official_Languages.pdf| access-date =October 2, 2009 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080625231116/http://www.justice.gov.nt.ca/PDF/ACTS/Official_Languages.pdf|archive-date = June 25, 2008}}</ref> Besides English and French, these languages are not vehicular in government; official status entitles citizens to receive services in them on request and to deal with the government in them.<ref name="online" />

===Visual art===
{{Further|Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas}}
[[File:Metis shawl.JPG|thumb|alt=A colour photograph of a young girl in a traditional shawl between two adults|A young [[Métis]] girl wearing a traditional [[shawl]]]]

[[Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Indigenous peoples were producing art]] for thousands of years before the arrival of European [[Settler colonialism|settler colonists]] and the eventual establishment of Canada as a [[nation state]]. Like the peoples who produced them, Indigenous art traditions spanned territories across North America. Indigenous art traditions are organized by art historians according to cultural, linguistic or regional groups: Northwest Coast, [[Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Plateau|Plateau]], [[Plains Indians|Plains]], [[Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands|Eastern Woodlands]], Subarctic, and Arctic.<ref name="art" />

Art traditions vary enormously amongst and within these diverse groups. Indigenous art with a focus on portability and the body is distinguished from European traditions and its focus on architecture. Indigenous visual art may be used in conjunction with other arts. Among Inuit the [[Masks among Eskimo peoples|masks]] and rattles of the ''[[angakkuq]]'' ([[Shamanism|shaman]]) are used ceremoniously in dance, storytelling and music.<ref name="art" >{{cite book |last=Hessel |first=Ingo |author2=Hessel, Dieter |title=Inuit Art: An introduction |year=1998 |publisher=[[British Museum]] Press |location=London |isbn=978-0-7141-2545-9 }}</ref> Artworks preserved in museum collections date from the period after European contact and show evidence of the creative adoption and adaptation of European trade goods such as metal and glass beads.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/aboriginal-art-in-canada|title=Aboriginal art in Canada|encyclopedia=The Canadian Encyclopedia |publisher= Historica-Dominion | access-date =November 27, 2013}}</ref> The distinct Métis cultures that have arisen from inter-cultural relationships with Europeans contribute culturally hybrid art forms.<ref name="Hempstead2010">{{cite book|first=Andrew |last=Hempstead|title=Moon Alberta: Including Banff, Jasper & the Canadian Rockies|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U3U-WpBsL80C&pg=PA477|date=May 11, 2010|publisher=Avalon Travel|isbn=978-1-59880-371-6|page=477}}</ref> During the 19th and the first half of the 20th century the Canadian government pursued an active policy of [[Forced assimilation|forced]] and cultural assimilation toward Indigenous peoples. The ''Indian Act'' banned manifestations of the [[Sun Dance]], the Potlatch, and works of art depicting them.<ref name="IA1880">{{cite web |title=An Act further to amend 'The Indian Act, 1880' |website=Indian and Northern Affairs Canada |date=March 21, 1881 |url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ai/arp/ls/pubs/d81c17/d81c17-eng.asp|access-date=October 18, 2009|archive-date=June 13, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613180222/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ai/arp/ls/pubs/d81c17/d81c17-eng.asp}}</ref>

[[File:Drumdance.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=Female dancer in costume performing in front of an audience|Dancer at Drum Dance Festival, [[Gjoa Haven]], [[Nunavut]]]]

It was not until the 1950s and 1960s that Indigenous artists such as [[Mungo Martin]], [[Bill Reid]] and [[Norval Morrisseau]] began to publicly renew and re-invent Indigenous art traditions. Currently, there are Indigenous artists practising in all media in Canada and two Indigenous artists, Edward Poitras and [[Rebecca Belmore]], have represented Canada at the [[Venice Biennale]] in 1995 and 2005 respectively.<ref name="art" />

===Music===
{{Main|Indigenous music of Canada}}

Indigenous peoples in Canada encompass diverse ethnic groups with their [[Indigenous music of Canada|individual musical traditions]]. Music is usually social (public) or ceremonial (private). Public, social music may be [[dance music]] accompanied by [[rattle (percussion instrument)|rattles]] and drums. Private, ceremonial music includes vocal songs with accompaniment on percussion, used to mark occasions like Midewivin ceremonies and [[Sun Dance]]s.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}}

Traditionally, Indigenous peoples used the materials at hand to make their instruments for centuries before Europeans immigrated to Canada.<ref name="second" >{{cite book|last=Patterson|first=Nancy-Lou|author-link=Nancy-Lou Patterson|title=Canadian native art; arts and crafts of Canadian Indians and Eskimos|year=1973|publisher=Collier-Macmillan|location=Don Mills, ON|isbn= 978-0-02-975610-2}}</ref> First Nations people made [[gourd]]s and animal [[Horn (anatomy)|horns]] into rattles, which were elaborately carved and brightly painted.<ref name="PDF">{{cite web| title = Information First Nations Music in Canada| work = Indian and Northern Affairs Canada| publisher = Minister of Public Works and Government Services Canada| url = http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ach/lr/ks/rrds/rrds_infsht_mus-eng.asp| format =PDF|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706181516/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/ach/lr/ks/rrds/rrds_infsht_mus-eng.asp|archive-date=July 6, 2011|access-date=May 13, 2013}}</ref> In woodland areas, they made horns of [[birch bark]] and [[Percussion mallet|drumsticks]] of carved antlers and wood. Traditional percussion instruments such as drums were generally made of carved wood and animal [[Hide (skin)|hides]]. These [[musical instrument]]s provide the background for songs, and songs the background for dances. Traditional First Nations people consider song and dance to be sacred. For years after Europeans came to Canada, First Nations people were forbidden to practice their ceremonies.<ref name="IA1880"/><ref name="second" />

==Demography==
{{Further|Population of Canada#Indigenous peoples|Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas}}
{{See also|List of First Nations peoples in Canada|List of Indian reserves in Canada|List of Canadian census divisions with Indigenous majority populations}}
[[File:Indigenous population by census division.svg|thumb|left|upright=1.5|Percent reporting indigenous identity by census division as of the [[2021 Canadian census|2021 census]].]]

There are three ([[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]],<ref name="First Nations Culture Areas Index" /> [[Inuit]]<ref name="ICCcharter" /> and [[Métis#Métis people in Canada|Métis]]{{sfn|Todd|Thornton|Collins|2001|p=10}}) distinctive groups of Indigenous peoples that are recognized in the Canadian ''Constitution Act, 1982'', [[Section 25 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|sections 25]] and 35.<ref name="defe"/> Under the ''[[Employment equity (Canada)|Employment Equity Act]]'', Indigenous people are a designated group along with women, visible minorities, and persons with disabilities;<ref>{{cite web| title = Canadian Human Rights Commission :: Resources :: Frequently Asked Questions :: About Employment Equity| work = Canadian Human Rights Commission| publisher =Government of Canada| date = August 27, 2009| url = http://www.chrc-ccdp.ca/publications/ee_faq_ee-en.asp#1| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927003006/http://www.chrc-ccdp.ca/publications/ee_faq_ee-en.asp| archive-date = September 27, 2007| access-date =September 18, 2009}}
</ref> as such, they are neither a [[visible minority]] under the ''Act'' or in the view of [[Statistics Canada]].<ref>{{cite web|title = Classification of visible minority|publisher = Statistics Canada |via=statcan.gc.ca|date = July 25, 2008|url = http://www.statcan.gc.ca/concepts/definitions/minority01-minorite01a-eng.htm|access-date = September 18, 2009|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110714060402/http://www.statcan.gc.ca/concepts/definitions/minority01-minorite01a-eng.htm|archive-date = July 14, 2011|df = mdy-all}}</ref>

The [[2021 Canadian census|2021 Census]] data reveals that there are over 1.8 million Indigenous people in Canada, comprising 5.0% of the overall population and a slight increase from 4.9% in 2016.<ref name="t481">{{cite web | title=Canada's Indigenous population | website=Statistics Canada | date=2023-06-21 | url=https://www.statcan.gc.ca/o1/en/plus/3920-canadas-indigenous-population | access-date=2024-12-18}}</ref>

The growth of the Indigenous population has slowed compared to previous years. The population grew by 18.9% between 2011 to 2016, while the growth from 2016 to 2021 was only 9.4%. For the first time, the Census recorded more than 1 million First Nations people living in Canada. The Indigenous population continues to grow at a faster rate than the non-Indigenous population but at a reduced speed. The Indigenous population is projected to reach between 2.5 million and 3.2 million in the next 20 years.<ref name="t481"/>

The First Nations population overall increased by 9.7% from 2016 to 2021. However, Status First Nations saw a slower growth of 4.1%, compared to those without Registered Indian status, which grew by 27.2%. The Métis population rose by 6.3%, and the Inuit population grew by 8.5%. More than half of First Nations people (55. 5%) lived in Western Canada as of 2021. Ontario had the highest number of First Nations people, with 251,030 (about 23.9%) of the total First Nations population. Approximately 11.1% of First Nations people lived in Quebec, with 7.6% in Atlantic Canada and 1.9% in the territories.<ref name="t481"/>

The 2021 Census showed nearly three in four Canadians lived in urban areas, with 801,045 Indigenous people living in large urban centers. This is an increase of 12.5% from 2016, signifying that Indigenous people were more likely to reside in these areas compared to before.<ref name="t481"/>

Moreover, the Indigenous population is generally younger than the non-Indigenous population. In 2021, the average age of Indigenous people was 33.6 years, compared to 41.8 years for non-Indigenous people. The Inuit population was the youngest, averaging 28.9 years, followed by First Nations at 32.5 years and Métis at 35.9 years. In total, there were 459,215 Indigenous children aged 14 years and younger, making up 25.4% of the Indigenous population, while only 16.0% of the non-Indigenous population fell into this age category.<ref name="t481"/>

In the 20th century, the Indigenous population of Canada increased tenfold.<ref name="statcan_aboriginal_demographics">{{cite web| title = Aboriginal peoples of Canada: A demographic profile| publisher = Statistics Canada| via = statcan.gc.ca| year = 2001| url = http://www12.statcan.ca/english/census01/Products/Analytic/companion/abor/canada.cfm| access-date = October 2, 2009| archive-date = May 17, 2008| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080517064517/http://www12.statcan.ca/english/census01/products/analytic/companion/abor/canada.cfm/}}</ref> Between 1900 and 1950 the population grew by 29%. After the 1960s the [[infant mortality]] level on reserves dropped dramatically.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vancouverprofile.com/aboutvancouver/content.php/id/2221|title=Aboriginals First Nations |website=vancouverprofile.com |access-date=October 15, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100616164320/http://www.vancouverprofile.com/aboutvancouver/content.php/id/2221|archive-date=June 16, 2010}}</ref><ref name=babies/> Since the 1980s, the number of First Nations babies more than doubled and in 2009 almost half of the First Nations population was under the age of 25.<ref name="statcan_aboriginal_demographics" /><ref name=babies>{{cite web |url=http://www12.statcan.ca/english/census01/Products/Analytic/companion/abor/canada.cfm |title=Aboriginal peoples of Canada |publisher=Statistics Canada |via=statcan.gc.ca |access-date=October 5, 2009 |archive-date=May 17, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080517064517/http://www12.statcan.ca/english/census01/products/analytic/companion/abor/canada.cfm/ }}</ref>

Indigenous people assert that their [[Sovereignty|sovereign rights]] are valid, pointing to the [[Royal Proclamation of 1763]], which is mentioned in the Canadian ''Constitution Act, 1982'', Section 25, the ''[[British North America Acts]]'' and the [[Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties|1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties]] (to which Canada is a signatory) in support of this claim.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ohlj.ca/archive/articles/34_1_mcneil.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706191452/http://www.ohlj.ca/archive/articles/34_1_mcneil.pdf |archive-date=July 6, 2011 |first=Kent |last=McNeil |title=Aboriginal Governments and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms |publisher =Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples |page=73 |year=1996| access-date =October 6, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/PreConfederation/rp_1763.html |title=The Royal Proclamation |work= By The King George R. A Proclamation | access-date =October 6, 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091013182626/http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/PreConfederation/rp_1763.html| archive-date=October 13, 2009| url-status=live}}</ref>

===Geographical distribution===

[[Ethnography|Ethnographers]] commonly classify Indigenous peoples of the Americas in the United States and Canada into ten geographical regions, [[Classification of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas|cultural areas]], with shared cultural traits.<ref>{{cite web| website=Civilization.ca |title=Gateway to Aboriginal Heritage-Culture Areas Index| publisher=Canadian Museum of Civilization Corporation| date = May 12, 2006| url = http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/tresors/ethno/etb0170e.shtml| access-date =October 6, 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091020033621/http://www.civilization.ca/cmc/exhibitions/tresors/ethno/etb0170e.shtml| archive-date=October 20, 2009| url-status=live}}</ref> The Canadian regions are:
* [[Inuit|Arctic cultural area]] ([[Eskaleut languages]])
* [[Indigenous peoples of the Subarctic|Subarctic culture area]] ([[Na-Dene languages]] and [[Algic languages]])
* [[Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands|Eastern Woodlands (Northeast) cultural area]] ([[Algic languages]] and [[Iroquoian languages]])
* [[Plains Indians|Plains cultural area]] ([[Siouan languages|Siouan–Catawban languages]])
* [[Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Plateau|Northwest Plateau cultural area]] ([[Interior Salish languages]])
* [[Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast|Northwest Coast cultural area]] ([[Penutian languages]], [[Tsimshianic languages]] and [[Wakashan languages]])

====Urban population====
Across Canada, 56% of Indigenous peoples live in urban areas. The urban Indigenous population is the fastest-growing population segment in Canada.<ref name="aadnc-aandc.gc.ca">{{cite web|url=https://www.aadnc-aandc.gc.ca/eng/1100100014265/1369225120949 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171101183603/https://www.aadnc-aandc.gc.ca/eng/1100100014265/1369225120949 |archive-date=November 1, 2017 |url-status=deviated |title=Urban Indigenous peoples |website=Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada |language=en |access-date=October 31, 2017 |date=November 21, 2008}}</ref>
